en: A line about who you are
The smith needs raw iron. Bring back ore from the surrounding hills.
Holt's barrels come up from Hollowreach and this month they did not. Walk down to the wharf and find out from Sedge Marrow whether they are coming at all.
Ask Sedge Marrow about the barrels
and the two quests that call them ---
Sedge Marrow will not send her season's ledger up the road with a stranger, and she will not send it alone either. Walk her hull-hand Tessa Rill to Embermarket and see her there in one piece.
See Tessa Rill safely to Embermarket
The warband wants the north road held long enough for a cart to clear it. Stand in the wilds north of the Ember Crown for a full minute and do not be moved off it.

Coyle Ferrin's month of figures is sealed in a tin and due at the Emberdeep waystone before the shift changes. The short way north is open ground, and the goblins on it do not need to know what you are carrying.
Set the tally at the Emberdeep waystone
Reach the mine without being drawn into a fight
Goblins harry the roads out of the Ember Crown. The guild posts a standing bounty: thin their numbers in the wilds.
Bryn's forge runs cold without ore. Bring iron from the northern hills so the smith can arm the town.
Mirela's stores run thin while goblin wounds mount. Gather healing herb from the wilds for the apothecary.
The goblins answer to a warband massing in the northern wilds. The elder asks you to break its back before it falls on the town.

keys: # --- Phase 34.5C: the Frostfang clan arc and its betrayal branch ---

en: Hjalvar Stormbound will not take an outsider's word for anything. The rime that drifts down from the passes is a problem the hold has stopped bothering to name. Break four of them.
Sigrun counts the stores twice and does not like the second number. Pelts, off whatever will spare them, before the long dark closes the passes.
What Comes Up Through the Ice
Something walks the ice that stopped being anyone a long time ago. The clans have a word for the Hollow and it is not a polite one. Put five of them down.
Halvar One-Hand watches the hold's fires from outside them and has an offer for anyone the hold has not yet claimed. Three of their raiders, and he will believe you mean it.
The shamans are what hold the clans together in the cold. Halvar wants two of them silenced, and has a buyer in the south who wants the same.
The notice board bristles with contracts. One fresh bounty catches your eye.
BOUNTY: Goblins prey on our roads. Cull three in the wilds and the guild pays in coin. Take the contract?
The contract is yours. Goblins haunt the wilds beyond the walls — go earn your coin.
The bounty still stands: three goblins, not yet culled.
The bounty is settled — the guild thanks you. Watch the board for more.

en: so nothing reaches the quest log or the story flags.
A slab of oak nailed with proclamations, half of them faded to nothing. Three are still legible.

BY ORDER OF THE TOWN: no blade drawn between the lamps. No fire but the braziers. Weights are the town's and are checked at dawn. Any trader found short-weighing forfeits his stall and his stock, and the Dawnwardens will see him to the gate.

NOTICE: the Crossway Post now takes a toll of every cart that comes south. The road wardens say it pays for the road. The carters say it pays for the wardens. Either way, what arrives here arrives dearer than it did last season.

STALL HOLDERS, EMBERMARKET: every stall on this square stands let and unclaimed, awaiting the season's traders. Coin, cloth, iron, herb, hide and glass. Enquiries to the town, who will want to know your trade before your name.
Bryn looks up from a cold anvil, soot dark on his brow.
The forge — is it burning again?
My forge is dead without ore. Bring me three lumps of iron from the hills and I'll keep the town in steel. Will you?
Bless you. The hills lie to the north — mind the goblins along the way.
Still cold, this forge. Three lumps of iron ore — that's all I ask.
The iron you brought has the forge roaring again. Steel for the town at last — my thanks.
Mirela grinds herbs with a worried frown, her shelves near bare.
Goblin wounds fill my cot and my remedies run dry. Four sprigs of healing herb from the wilds would save lives. Will you gather them?
Thank you. The herb grows in the wilds — look for the pale green leaves.
My shelves are still bare. Four sprigs of healing herb, when you can.
With these herbs the wounded will mend. You've done more than you know — thank you.
These raids are no accident. A warband masses in the northern wilds, and its captain means to burn us out. Cut down five of them and you break its nerve. Will you stand for the Ember Crown?
Then the Flame go with you. Strike at the heart of them in the northern wilds.
The warband still gathers. Five of them, traveller — break their nerve.
You broke the warband. The Ember Crown will sing your name by the hearth tonight — take the smith's finest steel, you have more than earned it.

en: Smoked fish out of Tarn's Landing
Aldreth straightens a row of jars across a counter with more bare wood than goods on it.

Thin is a kind word for it. The salt cart is nine days late and the last one before that came half empty, driver white as a sheet and no talk out of him. Whatever's sitting on the roads, it eats better than we do.
I'll keep an eye on the road.
The Iron King's fire guts the air where he fell, a fragment of fallen divinity beating like a second heart. It is yours to take. Will you absorb the flame?
Power floods you, hot and total, and somewhere far back something dims to make room for it. The bargain is struck.
You turn from it. The fire gutters, unclaimed, and the cold rushes back in to fill the dark.
Level up!  You are now level {0}
Kael Aldemar will not take a stranger at his back. Cut down the goblins raiding the wilds and he will judge for himself what you are.
Cut down goblins in the wilds
Kael's sword-brother Toren fell in the northern wilds, and the goblins picked the Emberguard dead. Recover what they carried off.
The knight looks up from a whetstone and a blade that needs no sharpening.
Kael Aldemar. Last shield of the Emberguard, for whatever that's worth now. The order burned with the rest — I'm what the fire left standing.
You look like you're waiting for something.
I'm waiting to see what you do. Goblins are bleeding the roads while the guild counts coin. Cut four of them down out in the wilds. Then we'll talk about walking together.
I fight for my own reasons.
Good. Don't come back and tell me about it. Come back having done it.
Then the roads still bleed. Go.
I heard. The road's quieter than it was yesterday — that's not nothing. Say the word and my shield goes where you go.
Sworn, then. Not to a crown — to you. Try not to make me regret the difference.
Toren. My sword-brother. He held the pass at Ashfall so the rest of us could run, and the goblins picked his bones after. What they carried off is out there in their camps. I'd have it back.
Their camps are north. Take what they took.
I found what the ash left.
That's his. That's — yes. Twelve years I carried that pass, and I couldn't put it down. You reached back for a dead man you never met. I'll not forget it.
It's enough. He's carried now. Ask me for anything.
Do you ever think about stopping?
Every day. Then I look at where we're going and I think: someone has to walk in first. Might as well be the one who's already burned.
As you say. I'll be here, sharpening a blade that doesn't need it. Come back when you need a shield.
For a thousand years the world has been dying.
The gods are dead. Magic fades. Dragons have gone from the skies.
Seven champions were made to set it right. The Flamebearers.
Six fell — to corruption, to power, to the enemy itself.
You are the seventh, {0}. The last hope of Embervale, or its last ruin.
Move the mouse to look around
Press {0} and the surrounding keys to walk
Look at someone and press {0} to speak or use
Press {0} to open your character screen
Press {0} to read your quest journal
Press {0} to cast your prepared spell
The brazier is cold. The warband still holds the north.
The Iron King is ash, and his ember burns behind your ribs. It is warm. That is what frightens you.
The Iron King is ash. You let his ember go out — and felt, for a moment, how easy it would have been not to.
Far away, on a throne of ash, something older than a fallen king turns its attention towards you.
END OF ACT I.  Three more of the fallen hold the known realms: the Stormcrown in Frostfang, the Ashen Wilds beyond the Breach, and Sunspire past the Southmarch Gate.
The guild says you know every sword in this town.
Every one worth naming. Why — are you looking to share the road?

Then look for Kael Aldemar, in the square. Emberguard, before the Emberguard stopped being anything. He came back from Ashfall alone and he has been sharpening that blade ever since. Ask him yourself — he will not offer.
So I see. Good. He has carried that pass alone long enough — let him carry something forward instead.
You keep looking north like it owes you something.

I look north because I remember. A fallen champion's fire does not simply go out when you cut them down — it looks for a new hand to hold it. I have seen a man take that warmth for himself, meaning to do good with it. We buried what was left of who he had been. If you ever stand over one of them with the choice in front of you, remember that he meant well too.

keys: # --- Phase 33D: elder conversation moved off literals (CLAUDE.md §6) ---

en: (Greet the elder like an old friend.)
I'm still searching for that iron.
(Clasp his hand — your heart is still your own.)
(He flinches at your gaze. Ask what troubles him.)
The Flame keeps us both, elder.
(Say nothing. Let the ember within stir.)
Well met, traveller. Our smith's forge runs cold — we've no iron to feed it.
Three lumps of iron ore from the northern hills would set us right. Will you help?
Bless you. The hills lie to the north — mind the goblins along the way.
The forge still waits. Three lumps of ore — you'll find them in the hills to the north.
You brought the iron — the forge burns bright again. The village won't forget it.
Good to see you again, friend. The forge runs hot, thanks to you.
The elder meets your eyes and nods slowly. 'A steady soul — rarer than iron, these days. The Flame keeps you, traveller.'
'There is an ember in your gaze I do not trust — ash where the light should be. I have seen it before, and it does not end gently. Tread carefully, traveller.'
A broad man in wolf-hide watches you cross his hold without rising. 'Southerner. You walked in through the cold, so you are either useful or lost.'

'The Stormbound hold it, and eight clans besides — hunters, tamers, shamans. We do not answer to your guilds and we do not sit in your councils. Out here a name is what you carry, not what you are given.'
'Fear is a soft word. The Storm Tyrant took the high passes and calls it grief. He was a Flamebearer once, same as your Iron King. They all end the same way — certain.'
She looks you over the way she'd look over a sled dog — teeth first. 'Stores are counted. Twice.'
Do the clans trade with outsiders?
'With outsiders who have stood a winter here, yes. You have stood an afternoon. Come back when the hold knows your name and we will talk about what is mine to give.'
Something large shifts in the dark behind her and settles again at a word you don't catch. 'Stand still. They judge quickly.'
'No. Frost-stalkers, whelped and raised. A hound obeys. These agree, for a while, and the day they stop agreeing is a day you want to be elsewhere.'
'Not the way you mean. The Sylthari sing at them and call it conversation. I feed them, I bleed for them, and I do not lie to them. That is the whole of it.'
The old man feeds the fire without looking up. 'Sit or don't. The cold has no opinion either way.'
'Older than the Ember Crown's walls, and it was never besieged, because there was never anything here worth the march. Ask me again when your south has burned down twice.'
'There is always work. Whether it is yours is a different question.'
He does not stand, but he moves along the bench, which from him is a ceremony. 'Sit. You carried what you said you would. The hold has your name now and it will not give it back.'

'Rime drifts down from the high passes and cuts whoever walks into it. We step around it. That is what stepping around a thing for twenty years looks like — a hold that has stopped calling it a problem. Break four. Then we will talk about what you are.'
'They do not bleed and they do not tire. Hit them until they stop being a shape.'
'Four. The passes are north of here and the cold does the counting.'
'Cleared. Twenty years and a stranger does it in an afternoon.' He does not sound pleased, exactly. 'The hold will use your name now. Do not make us regret teaching it.'

'Husks. They come up through the ice where the ice is thin, and they were people once, which is the part the young ones cannot get past. Five of them. Do not look at their faces and you will be fine.'
'Good. Yrsa will not send the stalkers after them — they will not go. That should tell you something.'
'Still walking, are they. Then you are not finished.'
'Done, and done without asking what it was worth first.' He is quiet a moment. 'You eat at the hearth from tonight. That is not a small thing and I will not say it twice.'
'I did. And here you are, with the hold using your name like it always did.' She sets down the tally. 'So. Stores.'

'Pelts. Five, off whatever out there can spare them, and I do not mean the stalkers — those are Yrsa's and she counts them too. The passes close in a month and a hold that is short in a month is a hold that is short all winter.'
'Wolves off the ice will do. Bring them whole — I can tell when a thing was skinned in a hurry.'
'Five. I said five and the number has not moved since.'
She weighs them the way she weighed you, and this time nods. 'Sworn to the stores, then. You are on the tally now — which means when it is short, it is partly your fault. Welcome to it.'
'I heard. They have not settled on you yet — but they stopped watching the door when you came through it, and that is most of the way there.'
Sigrun has me on the tally.
The old man finally looks up. 'Sworn to the stores. That is the one that counts, whatever the chief says over his bench. A hold is what it has in the cellar when the passes shut.'
and the branch that sells them out
A man sits at a fire too far from the hold's to be an accident, warming one hand and a stump. 'Southerner. You are the first thing to walk this way in a season that was not weather.'

'Hjalvar happened to it. There was a judgement, and there were eight clans in the room, and none of them was mine by the end of it.' He turns the stump to the fire. 'I do not dispute the judgement. I dispute surviving it out here.'
'I want the hold to be smaller. There are men in the south who want the same thing and pay for it, which makes us partners rather than friends.'

'It is. The rites are broken and the hold knows exactly whose hand did it — both of ours, and only one of us is easy to find.' He almost smiles. 'The Syndicate has your name now. That is worth more than mine and costs about the same.'

'Three of their raiders. Not for the killing — for the proof. Everyone who comes to this fire says they owe the hold nothing, and every one of them walks back down to it by dark. Three, and I will believe you.'
No. They've done nothing to me.
'Understand what you have agreed to. They will not forget it and there is no judgement out here to appeal to. There is only what you can carry.'
'Three. The patrols run the low ground by day and they do not look up.'

'Three, and you came back to say so.' He counts coin into the snow rather than your hand. 'The Syndicate keeps names. Yours is on a list now, and lists are the closest thing to a clan you will get south of here.'
'Two shamans. Raiders are replaceable — every hold breeds more. The rites are not. Kill the storm out of them and the eight clans are eight cold camps arguing about firewood by spring.'
'They call the weather down on you before they close. Do not let them finish. That is the whole of the advice I have.'
'Two. And you will hear the second one coming — they never learn not to sing.'
He listens to the wind for a while, which is only wind now. 'Twenty years I sat here waiting for that quiet. It is not what I thought it would sound like.' The coin comes anyway.

keys: # Names for the three bespoke-factory creatures (Phase 34G — were hard-coded English)
# Bestiary (BestiaryPanel) — the Ash Hunters' field journal

en: Seen, not yet understood. {0} more to fill the page.
Scavengers of the valley's edge, bold in numbers and cowardly alone. They have no forges of their own; every blade they carry was somebody else's first.
Ashfall's roads emptied of soldiers long before they emptied of travellers. These are the people who noticed. Fast, poorly armoured, and never encountered singly.
They call the burning a mercy. Zealots of the Fallen do not retreat, do not bargain, and do not appear to feel the fire they carry.
Armour still bearing a dead lord's colours, worn by something that no longer answers to him. They hold a shield line out of habit — the habit outlasted the man.
The Iron Syndicate does not send warnings. An enforcer waits without moving for as long as the contract requires, and the first sign of one is usually the last.
They do not charge. They fan wide, take the flanks, and wait for the pack-mate you turned your back on. Killing the first one teaches you nothing about the other three.
Twice the mass of the pack it leads and slower for it, which matters less than you would hope. Ash Hunters price a dire wolf pelt at four ordinary ones and still consider it cheap.
Frostfang's cats do not stalk so much as wait, buried to the eyes, for a week if need be. Struck first it dies easily. It is rarely struck first.
Blind past ten paces and entirely uninterested in you until you are inside that ten. Then it does not stop, does not tire, and does not recognise a wound as an argument.

An old thornback, three-legged since some earlier argument it won at a cost. It has held the same stretch of the deadfall for longer than the lodge has stood, and it has never once followed anyone out of it.
Grazes the grey meadows where nothing else will. It runs long before it is threatened and cannot be caught on foot — the hide is worth the arrow it costs.
What the Hollow Queen leaves when she is finished. It notices you late, and then it simply does not stop coming. There is no fear left in it to work with.
It still keeps the guard rhythm it was drilled in — up, down, up — long after the flesh that learned it went. Wait out the cycle. It cannot break the habit and it will not retreat.
Lies in the ground where it was laid and does not stir for the passing. It stirs for the digging. Whatever it was buried with, it still counts as its own.
Kill the husks and she knits them back together; kill her and they stay down. Every Ash Hunter learns this in the same order, and most learn it the wrong way round first.
Cold, quick and barely there — three of them will surround you before one of them touches you. Steel finds them, which is the only mercy in it.

Set to guard something by a civilisation that has been dust for an age. It has not been relieved, so it is still on duty. The wind-up before it swings is long enough to read, and that is the whole fight.
Bound to a doorway rather than a master. Arcane force slides off it — a fact worth knowing before you commit to a spell — and it will come apart before it will step aside.
Small, fast, and never alone. Best understood as the ruin's immune response: individually trivial, collectively how expeditions end.
A knot of live fire that answers to nothing. Fighting one with flame is a lesson most only need once — it drinks what it is made of.
It does not chase. It freezes the ground you were going to stand on and waits for you to arrive there anyway.
Its lightning does not stop at the first target. Fight one at a distance from your companions, or fight it twice.
Not a creature so much as a spell that outlived its caster and kept the intent. It wards itself unprompted, and it strips whatever ward you were relying on.
A beast the corruption took whole. Whatever it used to be knew when to run; this does not. The Ash Hunters count it as game, but only just.
A Fallen who kept enough of themselves to cast and lost everything else. The lifedrain it works on you is the same rite the Marked are offered — it simply accepted first.
The lesser Fallen: robed, smouldering, and convinced. It throws fire because fire is all it has left to say.

The First Flamebearer. He was given the ember to save the world and concluded that a world worth saving would have to be held still to do it. He is not wrong about the danger. He is wrong about everything after.

Shield, axe, and a patience the south mistakes for slowness. A raider will let you walk past a dozen times; the clans count a stranger's crossings before they count his coin. Start something and you learn what the shield was for.
She hunts the way her stalkers do — wide, quiet, and never quite where you looked. The beasts are not commanded so much as agreed with, which is worse: cross her and there is no order to countermand.
The clans do not pray to Nyth. They listen to the weather and answer it, and what answers back is cold enough to stop a heart mid-beat. She mends her own before she ever turns the storm on you.

en: Older than the guilds, older than the Sundering, and entirely uninterested in either. A wild dragon claims a stretch of mountain and defends it against everything that walks — no cause, no bargain, no god. The Ash Hunters' advice is one line long: it turns slowly.

keys: # Phase 35E — the Ash dragon. Its own creature
en: not a corrupted Wild one (see LORE "Ash Dragons").

What Morthul makes of a dragon. It does not hoard, it does not claim a mountain, it does not care that you are there — it simply keeps going until the ground behind it is grey. The Hunters have no advice for this one. There is no safe side.

keys: # Phase 35F — the Ancient dragon. The one creature in the bestiary the player can talk to.

en: There were never many, and there are fewer now. An Ancient does not hoard gold or hold a mountain; it holds words, which is the only thing left worth keeping from before the gods died. It will talk to you. That is not the same as it being safe, and the Ash Hunters would like it noted that the last party to test the difference is still up there.
The Ancient in the northern aerie will not go east itself. It says the thing in the ash roost was a dragon once, and that this is the sort of errand younger, shorter-lived things are for.
Kill the Ash dragon in the eastern roost

Halda Rieve has been casting the same print for four nights running: something heavy, favouring three legs, working the deadfall east of the lodge. Find what it is before you decide what to do about it.
Read the scraped bark in the deadfall
Read the wallow in the deadfall
Tell Halda Rieve what you found
Deal with Grimtusk, if that is the judgment
Bring word of the kill to Fell Ardan
Tell Halda Rieve the den is marked
The head comes down slowly, until one eye is level with you and considerably larger. 'You climbed all of that to look at me. Speak, then, small thing, and be interesting about it.'

'Old. That is the whole of it, and it took a very long time. I was here when the sky had gods in it and I was here the morning it did not. Your kind writes that down as an age. I remember it as weather.'
They say your kind keeps what the world forgot.

'Keeps. Yes. Not guards — nothing has come for it in eight hundred years. The Weave thins and your casters shout louder to be heard through it, and none of them think to ask the thing that learned to speak before the thinning started. So: keeps. Like a cellar keeps wine no one drinks.'

'I am looking at what is in you. I have seen that grey before, on my own kin, in the east. It does not stop, you understand. It is not a wound. It is an opinion the world is having about you, and it wins arguments slowly.'

'East of here, past the hold, something is sleeping in a roost that used to belong to a dragon. It still has the shape. Morthul is thorough about shapes. I will not go — I have watched enough of my kin become that, and I will not be the one who ends this one. You are younger. You have fewer things to remember afterward. Kill it.'
'Then go while you still think it is a favour to me. Take the cold seriously and the ash more so. It breathes rot, not fire — whatever you wore against my western cousin will not help you.'
The thing in the east still lives.
'I know. I would feel it stop. Go back down, or stay and talk — I have had centuries of practice at waiting and you have not.'

The great head turns aside for a long moment. 'I felt it. Thank you is a small word and I have not needed it in some time, so you will have the other kind of payment. There is one word I have never given away. It is not a spell your teachers could sell you; there is no one alive to sell it.'

It speaks, once, quietly, and the air between you disagrees about being air. When your ears work again the word is simply there, sitting behind your teeth, patient. 'Now there are two of us who know it. Do not be careless with the only copy.'

keys: # Phase 35G — the frost drake: the dragon you can meet by accident.

en: A dragon that never finished becoming one. Drakes do not fly, do not hoard and do not talk; they hold a stretch of snow and breathe cold at anything crossing it. The Ash Hunters rate them the most dangerous thing in the Reach that is not worth a song, and lose people to them every winter for exactly that reason.
It is already dead. I found the east roost before I found you.

keys: # 38L — the ten Embermarket merchant conversations. Each is dialogue.vendor_goods's shape:

and one talk node carrying a beat of what the economy arc is about to build.
A broad man in a flour-dusted apron sets down a tray of loaves without looking at it. "Morning. Bread's fresh, ration's honest, and I don't sell anything I wouldn't eat."

"Busier? Aye, it was. Two seasons back you couldn't cross this square without turning sideways." He shrugs. "Carts come south slower now, and dearer, and the folk who mind that most are the ones with nothing to sell but bread."
The trays are covered and the shutter is down. Corvin is somewhere behind it, asleep, and has been since the light went.
I'll take some of that bread.
A woman with forearms like cable slaps a split fish onto the slab. "You're early enough to matter. Come back after noon and you're buying yesterday."

"Tarn's Landing sends what it can, when the road lets it." She wipes the blade. "There's talk of the wharf down at Hollowreach selling cheaper. There's always talk. Cheaper fish usually means somebody didn't pay the toll."
The slab is scrubbed white and the ice is a puddle. Hana is long gone; she trades at dawn or not at all.
Where does the catch come from?
I'll take some before it's gone.
Bolts of cloth stand on end behind the counter like a rank of soldiers. "Linen, wool, and one red I'd not sell to just anyone. Look, don't finger."

"That red is madder, fixed with alum, and it costs what it costs." She turns a bolt to the light. "Every banner over this town started that colour. They go rose in a year and pink in three, and nobody replaces them any more, which tells you more about the Ember Crown than I'd care to say aloud."
The bolts are sheeted over against the damp and the shutter is barred from inside.
I'll buy a length of it.
A narrow man looks up over a pair of cracked spectacles, one finger keeping his place. "Books. Copies of books. Copies of copies, if you're not particular."

"There's a treatise under this counter I don't show strangers." He does not look at where it is. "The Veiled Archive would rather it had stayed in the Archive. I'd rather know who I'm handing it to. Come back when the town knows your name."
The stall is shuttered and a chain runs through the handles. A card in the gap reads: BACK AT NINE.
Anything you don't put on the shelf?
Show me what you will sell.
Everything about him is grey except his hands, which are black to the wrist. "Charcoal, pitch, and whatever ore comes my way. Mind the sacks, they mark."

"Every forge in this town burns what I cut, and none of them think about it twice." He coughs. "There's a mine east of here they say is opening again. Emberdeep. If it does, I'll be buying ore by the cartload and you'll be able to tell, because the price of everything iron will fall through the floor."
The stall is a tarpaulin over a heap of sacks, roped down and unattended. Dunmore burns his kilns at night.
Iron bar is stacked to the counter's edge in graded rows. "I don't forge. I buy, I sell, and I know to the ounce what's in front of you. Bryn's up the hill if you want it beaten into something."

"Stall's mine, the stock isn't - not all of it." She raps the counter. "Half of what you see I hold on somebody else's coin, and I pay for the privilege. Anyone with money to put down and the sense to leave it down would find me a good deal more generous about what I keep in the back."
The bar stock is under a locked grille. A slate reads: SEVEN TILL SEVEN. NO CREDIT.

The smell arrives before the stall does. "Hides, strips, and a cap or two. If you've been out in the wilds and come back with anything skinned, I'm the best price in the realm and I'll not pretend otherwise."

"Month of work in a single sheet, that." He holds a hide up and lets the light through it. "Scraped, limed, cured, and every step of it something you can ruin. Folk think a tanner buys hides. A tanner buys a month and sells it back to you flat."
The frames are empty and the vats are covered. Whatever is curing under those lids will keep until seven.
How much work is in one?
Cloth-of-grey under glass, and on it four stones arranged with more care than most people give a meal. "Don't breathe on the sapphires."

"Everyone in this market thinks they know what their goods are worth." She does not look up from the loupe. "They know what they were paid last time. Those are different numbers and the difference is my living." She taps the brass scales at the end of her counter without looking at them. "Put your pack on those and I'll tell you what every piece of it is worth and who'll pay it. No charge. I'd rather you sold in the right place than came back telling me the market's crooked."
The glass is empty and the cloth is folded. Nessa keeps banker's hours and makes no apology for it.
Then show me what you have.
Bundles hang drying from every strut of the stall, and the man beneath them is half hidden by them. "Careful of your head. Everything here was alive this week."

"Mirela up in the square brews. I walk." He grins, missing a tooth. "She'll not go past the wall for a leaf and I'll not stand over a pot for six hours, so between us the town gets its remedies. Emberbloom only opens when the ash falls, which means the days I earn most are the days nobody else wants to be outside."
The bundles are in and the stall is a bare frame. Odo is out past the wall somewhere, or asleep.
Planks lean in a fan against the stall post, and a half-made crate sits on the counter with the pegs still proud. "Timber, or things made of timber. Take your pick."

"You've a holding of your own, I hear." He taps the crate. "Then you'll want more than planks. I sell the kits whole - crate, stand, brazier, bench - packed flat and pegged, so you carry them home and set them down where you like. Beats standing at a workbench for an afternoon, unless you enjoy that. Some do."
The plank fan is chained to the post and the counter is bare. Halvard works to the light and the light has gone.
He is weighing a sack of ore against a counterweight and does not look up. "Iron, coal, copper if you're quick. It comes out of the ground twenty feet behind you, so don't tell me what it's worth."

"Every cart that leaves here is worth three times what I'm paid for it by the time it reaches a market stall." He sets the weight down. "That's the trade, apparently. I dig it, somebody with a cart gets rich, and I get to hear about the price of bread."
The weighing shed is shuttered and the scales are chained. A board reads: FIVE TILL SEVEN. NO ORE SOLD AFTER DARK.
Doesn't sound like a good deal for you.
The store is one long counter and a wall of empty shelves. "If you're carrying food, I'm buying, and I'll pay better than anyone in the valley. If you're carrying ore, so is everyone."

"Nothing grows in a hole in the ground." She taps the ledger. "Every loaf, every sack of grain, every block of salt on this mountain came up that road on somebody's back, and I pay for the walk as well as the bread. Bring me a cartload and I'll make it worth the blisters."
The shutters are down and the ledger is locked in the strongbox. A chalked line reads: SIX TILL EIGHT.
Why pay over the odds for bread?
A long counter, an empty shelf behind it, and a ledger open at a page of names. "I don't buy. Understand that first and we'll get on."

"Every stall on this square can only pay you what's in their box that morning. I'm not paying you at all — I'm selling it for you, to somebody with deeper pockets than anyone here, and I take my eighteen out of what it fetches." She taps the ledger without looking down. "Three days. Then the counter behind me, not me. I keep the book; Halder keeps the coin. That way neither of us can be robbed of both."
The shelf is under a sheet and the ledger is locked. A card in the glass reads: LISTINGS TAKEN NINE TILL SIX. COLLECTIONS ANY HOUR AT THE COUNTER.
Why would I wait three days?
She is splitting an eel without looking at it. "Fresh off the boats, salted if you're travelling, roe if you've the coin. Say which and be quick, it's half gone already."

"Everything you can see, we pull out of that water." She nods at the tarn. "Everything else comes up the road, when the road lets it. Salt, rope, cloth, hooks — we buy the lot, and we pay what we're asked, because what else are we going to do?"
The curing sheds are shuttered and the racks are bare. A board reads: BOATS OUT AT FOUR. FISH GONE BY TWO.
Coils of tarred rope hang to the roof beam. "Cordage, cloth, pitch, hooks. If it holds a boat together I sell it, and if you've any to spare I'll buy it off you before you've finished asking."

"Don't bring me fish." He says it before you can. "Wenna's forty feet up the beach and she'll give you a better price than I would, because I've no earthly use for it. Bring me rope. Bring me cloth, iron, anything that burns. That I'll pay well for, and I mean well."
The chandlery is locked and the rope is under a tarpaulin. A chalked board reads: SIX TILL SEVEN.

Set, and nobody the wiser. That is the whole trick of it.
The seat of the realm. Its square holds the smith, the apothecary and the inn; the guild board stands at the south road.
Rows of stalls under awnings, a plaza at the north end, and the realm's densest run of trades — twelve merchants between the aisles and the forecourt.
The wardens' post on the road between the realms. Nothing crosses here without the toll, a permit, or a word with the man at the side of the gate.
Ore out of the hill and food in at any price. The factor sells the realm's cheapest metal; the quartermaster pays its best coin for a full pack of provisions.
A jetty, a smokehouse and a chandlery on the tarn's edge.
Boat-builders and salvagers in the low ground, and a bones table that will take your coin on a throw.

The Ash Hunters' field station on the rise above the scar road, watching the plateau.
A levelled shelf under the northern wall where the Fourth Flamebearer holds his ground.
The preserved city, kept in perfect repair at an evening that never ends.
The Hollow Queen's palace at the end of the processional way.
The one terrace at the realm's edge that still holds a whole floor. The way home stands behind it.

The highest dais in the ruined heaven. Someone must always sit upon it.

There is a clerk's way and there is my way. The clerk's way is you walk up there, you give Halloway the manifest, you pay what they say the duty is, and the barrels come out with your name in a book that never gets thrown away. My way is Odger Vane at the Landing has a boat and no paperwork, and by the third night the barrels are on Holt's floor and nobody wrote anything down at all."
I'll take the manifest up to the post.
I'll think about which of us I am.

"The honest road." She does not say it unkindly. "Halloway holds the impound key on the post's coin, and she is exactly as bribable as the coin is good, which is to say not very. Take the number, pay the duty, and be pleasant. The book will remember you, and one day that will be worth something or it will cost you, and neither of us gets to know which."

en: He is reading the gate ledger by the door of the keep, and he finishes the line he is on before he looks up.

"You're on my book, so I'll say it plainly: we are twelve on a road that needs forty, and the north end of it is worse every month. Stand your watches. Don't let anyone tell you the wall is the point. The people behind it are."

"Wardens' Watch. We hold the road so the valley can pretend it doesn't need holding." He closes the ledger over one finger. "If you're passing, pay the toll and go. If you're something else, I'll know soon enough — I generally do."
I'll leave you to the book.
Mail is spread across the bench in front of her, and she is going along it ring by ring with a pair of pliers.

"Anything of ours that comes back broken comes back to me, so I'd rather you didn't break it." She sets down the pliers. "Ask for what you need and I'll find it. Ask for what you'd LIKE and we'll be here all evening."
"This bench is the Watch's, and so is everything on it." She does not stop working. "There's a smith in the town who'll sell to anyone. I fit out wardens."
Do you sell any of that?
He has the duty board under one arm and the look of a man who has been interrupted twice already.
"Good. The captain writes the orders and I hand them out, which means I'm the one who hears about it when they go badly." He taps the board. "There'll be work on here for you. There always is."

"Duty board. Warden business." He turns it away from you, then reconsiders. "Unless you mean to make it yours. We're twelve on a road that needs forty, and the north end gets worse every month. Take the oath or don't - I've no patience for half a conversation."

"Good." Something in his shoulders lets go, just slightly. "Go find Bram Corrow, out by the well. He made rank the hard way, and he's the one who tells you what the oath actually costs - before the captain does."
"Fair enough." He doesn't push it. "The door doesn't lock. Come back when it looks different to you."
"Corrow tells me you held the corrie and didn't lose your head after. That's the job, more than any of this." He taps the board once, like a period at the end of a sentence.
He's re-stringing a bow by the well, unhurried about it, like a man who's learned patience costs less than it looks like it does.
"Guild business," he says, not looking up. "Talk to Danhal if you want in. I've got nothing for you until then."
He sets the bow down. "Warden." It still sounds like he's trying the word out on someone else.

"There's a party working the western corrie above the Tarn - travelers, maybe worse, nobody's sure yet. We hold them off, that's simple enough. What happens after isn't." He looks at you steady. "Some of us bring the wounded home and let the Tarn deal with its own. Some of us bring them back here and let the guild decide what they're owed. I've done it both ways. Which one are you?"
"Home, then." He nods once, like it's the answer he'd have given himself. "Hold the corrie till it's quiet. I'll be waiting on the road after."
"Here, then." His face doesn't change, but he takes a moment before he answers. "Hold the corrie till it's quiet. Don't lose anyone bringing them in."
"Corrie's still that way," he says, nodding west. "Hold it. The rest comes after."
He sets the bow across his knees and waits for you to say it.
"Word from Tarn is they're settled," he says. "Whatever this cost you, they'll never know your name for it. That's usually how it goes."
"They're processed," he says, and doesn't elaborate. "The captain's satisfied. Whether you are is your business, not the guild's."
Get them home. That's the job.
Bring them here. Let the guild answer for it.
It's done. I got them home.
It's done. I brought them in.
Hold the western corrie against whatever is working it, then decide what becomes of the ones you take.
Hold the corrie above the Tarn
Escort the survivors home to Tarn Landing
Bring the survivors in to the Wardens' Watch

keys: # Phase 42D — the Dawnwardens' command arc and payoff.

en: He waits until you're both alone by the well before he says anything.

"Warrant-rider out of the Citadel. Iron King's own seal, if you believe the wax." He spits, once, off to the side. "Wants Sella Ru handed over for questioning about a granary fire at Tarn's Landing. Doesn't want to say what happens to her after. I want her here, talking to Danhal, before he decides for her."

"Warrant-rider, seal and all, still riding on a dead king's authority because nobody's told the Citadel clerks to stop stamping it." He shakes his head. "Wants Sella Ru handed over for questioning about a granary fire at Tarn's Landing. I want her here, talking to Danhal, before some clerk decides for her instead."

Sella falls in beside you without a word, one hand still knotted in her shawl. Bram nods toward the road north. "Watch's this way. Mind the patrol - the warrant-rider's men have been leaning on travelers all week."
"Get her to the Watch," he says. "Whatever's waiting on the north road after that, hold it."

"She gave her account. Danhal's got it in writing now, which is more than the warrant-rider bargained for." He almost smiles. "You held the road too. That's a warden's work, not a probationer's - I've told the captain as much."
It's settled, one way or another.

"He's back, and this time it's signed by someone who outranks Danhal." Bram's voice is flat. "Fold the Watch under Citadel command, or the Citadel declares us in default of it - which they're already calling treason, in the part of the order they didn't read aloud. Someone has to answer him. That's you, now."
We hold the corrie. Ourselves, this time.
We fold. Hand them the accused and keep the Watch standing.

"Then we hold it. Properly, this time - not a rescue, a stand." He checks the edge of his blade like it matters more than it does. "The corrie above the Tarn. If they want the people there, they go through us first."
He doesn't argue with you, which is somehow worse than if he had. "Bring them to the Watch, then. I'll tell Danhal what's coming."
"You know which way you chose," he says. "See it through."
He's waiting by the well again, like the first day, except he isn't re-stringing anything now.
We held the corrie. Nobody went through us.
It's done. The Watch stands. The rest is the Citadel's business now.

"Word's already out along the north road," he says. "A warden order that stood a line for people with no seal and no rank. Might be the most Dawnwarden thing anyone's done in years. Might also be the last time the Citadel asks us nicely."
"The Watch is still standing, and that was the point," he says, not quite meeting your eye. "The Citadel's satisfied. I keep telling myself that's the job."
She walks with her arms crossed tight over her shawl, flinching at every sound off the treeline that isn't a footstep.
"The Watch." She lets her arms drop for the first time since Tarn's Landing. "I can talk to the Serjeant myself from here."
An Iron Citadel warrant-rider wants Sella Ru handed over for a fire she only witnessed. Get her to the Wardens' Watch to give her account, then hold the north road against whatever answers that.
Escort Sella Ru to the Wardens' Watch
The Citadel wants the Wardens folded under its command or declared in default of it. Decide what the Dawnwardens are before someone else decides it for them.
Hold the corrie above the Tarn - yourselves, this time
Bring the accused to the Wardens' Watch
How's the Watch, since the warrant?
"Since the warrant, patrols have been asking after you by name," Danhal says. "Which one you want to hear about."

"Patrols out that way ride heavier now - two wardens instead of one, and they stop for anyone standing in the road." He allows himself something close to a smile. "The Citadel hasn't sent another rider. I don't expect that's over."
"Patrols out that way check papers twice now, where they used to check once." He doesn't quite meet your eye either. "The Citadel hasn't sent another rider. I don't expect that's a reward."
"The Citadel still writes to me like I answer to it," Fenn says. "I let the clerks think what they like. Ask what you came to ask."

"We stood a line the Citadel didn't authorize, and the roof is still on this Watch." He says it like a fact he's still testing the weight of. "Recruitment's up. So is the correspondence asking why I haven't been recalled."
"We kept the Watch standing by giving the Citadel what it asked for." He holds your gaze a moment too long before looking away. "I won't pretend that cost nothing. I will say it's still standing."

keys: # The Iron Syndicate — the Ledger House

en: He is standing in the doorway out of the damp with a folded contract in his hand, and he looks at you the way he would look at a figure in a column.

"Our arrangement stands, which is more than most people in this district can say about anything." He unfolds the contract and folds it again. "Terms, payment, and an ending everybody agreed to in advance. That is the whole of our creed and I have never needed a longer one."
"The Ledger House. We take work, we finish work, we are paid for work." The contract goes into his coat. "No one here will ask you to believe in anything. It is restful, once you get used to it."
He is sitting on a crate with a tally stick and a stub of chalk, and he keeps counting while you stand there.
"Whatever the work needs, I can get. Whatever the work leaves over, I can lose." He blows chalk dust off the stick. "Both of those are the same job and only one of them is written down."
"I count crates for a man who counts contracts." The chalk does not stop. "If you're after something you can buy in a market, go to a market."

keys: # The Ash Hunters — the Deadfall Lodge
en: under the scarp in the northern wilds.
She is under the lodge roof with a field book open on her knee, and she marks her place with a thumb before she answers.

"You're one of mine, so you already know the rule and I'll say it again anyway: the kill is the smallest part of it." She turns the book toward you — a drawing, a measurement, a date. "What you knew before you drew the bow is what I'll judge you on."

"The Deadfall. We track what comes down out of the wilds and we write down what we learn about it." The book closes. "Most people who find this place are looking for a trophy. We are not a trophy hall."
Who keeps a lodge out here?
He is working a hide over a frame with short, even strokes, and the smell of the racks is on everything.
"Bring me what you take and I'll make it worth carrying. Bring me what you were given and I'll know." He runs a thumb along the grain. "Hide remembers how the animal died. So do I."
"Racks are the lodge's. Hides are the lodge's." He does not look over. "There's a curer down at the Landing who'll take anything off anyone. I won't."
Would you work a hide for me?

He runs a hand along the hide you bring in, unhurried. "Old wound on the foreleg, half-healed and scarred hard — that's your three-legged track, and it explains the temper. Clean kill, by the look of it. Halda will want to know that part as much as the rest."
Then I'm one of yours properly now.
Bark stripped shoulder-high in a ragged band, on the uphill side of the trunk only. Whatever did it favours one side — the same side, going by the wear, every time it's come through here.

A wallow churned into the black earth, wide enough for something heavy, and a print at its rim gone soft at the edges — old, but not old enough to have washed out in this year's rain. Three-legged, like Halda said. The fourth print never sets.
She is crouched at the edge of the lodge floor with a cast of something's foot in front of her, and she turns it a quarter-turn as you come up.

"Something big came through the deadfall four nights ago and went back up the scarp on three legs." She sets the cast down. "That's the shape of the work here. It starts with a print and it ends a long way from one."
"Wouldn't stand on that side, you're in the light." She shifts the cast out of your shadow. "Ask me about it when you've a reason to know."
I'll get out of your light.

"Fair enough." She sets the cast down properly this time. "We don't take you on your word. Go find what's making a print, work out what it's worth doing about, and come back and tell me straight. That's the whole trial. No parade, no oath."
"Then you're one of ours as of now, not as of you finish something." She nods once, like that settles a private question. "Ask me what's moving. I'll tell you."
"Your business." She goes back to the cast without looking up again.

"Something big came through the deadfall and went back up the scarp on three legs, like I said. I've had four nights of it since and no cleaner a read." She taps the cast. "I'm not asking you to kill it. I'm asking you to find out what it is and what it's costing anyone, and then decide. That's the whole of the induction — knowing before you draw."
She turns the cast over once, unsurprised. "Word travels ahead of you, then. That's not the same as doing it right, but it's done, and I won't pretend otherwise. You're one of ours."
"Deadfall's east of the lodge, past where the pines close in. Don't go in blind — read the ground before you read the animal."

She sets the cast down and looks at you properly for the first time. "Then tell me. Is it a danger worth ending, or a territory worth marking off and leaving be? I'll back either. I want to hear which."
It's caused enough trouble. I'll finish it.
"Then finish it clean, not angry. Fell will want to see what's left of it after."
Let it be. I'll mark the den and warn people off.
She almost smiles. "That's the harder answer to give, and the one I hoped for less than half the time I ask it. Come back when the marker's up. I'll want to hear that too."
It's done. Fell has the hide.
"Good. That was the harder path and you took it clean — I heard as much from Fell before you got here."
The den's marked. I told people to keep clear.
"Then it's off my list, and you've earned your rank the way I'd rather see it earned — by knowing when not to draw."
She is standing in the Annexe door with her hands behind her back, in front of a room she does not move out of.

"Admission is granted once and it is never revisited, which is why we are careful about granting it." Her hands come apart. "What we hold, we hold because the world would rather it were gone. Read what you like. Copy nothing out of this room."

"A reading room. Nothing on the market's list." She does not move aside. "We are not a shop and we are not a library. A person joins us by bringing us something we did not have — and by not asking what happens to it afterwards."
There is ink to the second knuckle on both his hands, and a tray of ruled paper he is drying one sheet at a time.

"Ink, vellum, lamp oil, and a case that will keep a book dry between here and Frostfang." He lifts a sheet by its corner. "Everything the Keeper's work needs, and none of it is interesting, and all of it is the reason the work happens."
"The scriptorium in the market sells paper." He goes on drying. "This is the Annexe's, and the Annexe's is the Annexe's."
He has three books open at once on the Annexe's outer bench and is looking between them as though one of them is lying.

"Two of these say the ley line under the market runs north. The third was written by somebody who walked it." He taps the third. "So there is a thing to go and settle, and settling things is what the Keeper sends us out to do."
"Nothing to look at. Old arguments about old ground." He turns a page over, face down. "I'd tell you which ground, but then I'd have told you."
I'll leave you to your books.
off the Emberdeep pithead. A concealed order: the strangers'
which is the whole difference between this hub and the four public ones.
She is standing between two of the cut pillars with a lamp turned low, and she lets the silence go on a moment longer than is comfortable.

"You came down the stair, so somebody trusted you with the stair." The lamp comes up a little. "We study what the fire does to the people who carry it. Not whether it should be carried — that question has been used to justify everything ever done with it."
"You have come a long way down for a wrong turning." The lamp does not come up. "There is nothing worked in this part of the cut and there has not been for years. Go back up while the light holds."

She sets the lamp on the sill between you. "Bren doesn't send people down without reason, and I don't ask why he's right about them." A pause, weighing something. "We don't study the fire to decide who deserves it. We study what it does to whoever's already carrying it. You are. So — what happens to what you're carrying?"
Whatever it wants, it doesn't get it from me. Take it.
It stays with me. I started this; I'll finish it.
I didn't come down here to be studied.

She doesn't reach for anything — nothing changes hands here, not yet. "That's the harder answer, not the easier one." The lamp doesn't move. "Cass will ward it properly, in his own time. For now you've said the true thing out loud, and that's most of the work."

Her face doesn't change, which is its own kind of answer. "Then you'll carry it under our roof instead of alone. That's not nothing." The warmth goes out of her voice. "We don't take it from anyone who isn't offering. We tried that, once. It didn't end well for the one who tried."
Then I'm one of you, on those terms.
"Kindled, then." She says it like a fact rather than a welcome. "Bren will show you where the wall picks up. Cass will tell you what not to touch. I'll tell you the rest when there's a reason to."
She doesn't argue, and she doesn't look surprised. "Then this didn't happen." The lamp goes back down between you. "The stair's behind you, if that changes."
He is between you and the pedestal at the back of the chamber, and he has been standing there long enough that it looks like a habit.

"Everything we hold, I account for, and I account for it out loud." He shifts, just enough to show what is behind him. "An order that keeps relics and keeps no list of them stops being an order and becomes a hoard."
"There's nothing behind me." He does not move. "Miners come down here and take what isn't theirs. You'd not be the first, and I'd rather you weren't the next."
He is copying something off the chamber wall onto a wax tablet by the light of a single brazier, and he keeps his voice down out of habit rather than need.

"I go up and out and I come back with what nobody meant us to have." He angles the tablet toward the coals. "Half of it is a lie somebody carved to be found. The Hierarch says learning which half is the work."
"Old marks. Miners' marks." The tablet turns face down against his knee. "You get a lot of them in a cut this old."
I'll leave you to the wall.
You knew what was in the Iron King before it fell.

He sets the tablet down for the first time since you came in. "Word gets down here faster than boots do." His eyes go to your hands rather than your face. "What you're carrying isn't something to talk about at the bottom of a mine shaft. Go up. Come back when she'll see you — and she will."
"Good." He writes nothing down; the contract is the fact of you standing there. "Grieve has the ledger of what pays. Ask him."
"Suit yourself." He does not look up again. "The offer keeps. Most people change their minds once the winter does."

"Three jobs, three different ways to get paid, and you're still standing." He folds a fresh contract and does not hand it over — it is not for you to hold. "That is rank one. The Syndicate remembers who delivers."
"Bandits on the roads we're paid to keep clear. Three heads, gold on delivery — I don't need proof, I need them stopped." He taps the tally stick. "Straightforward. I like straightforward."
"Three, then. The road thanks you even if it never says so."
"Still three fewer bandits than I'd like. Go on."
"Quieter roads already. Whatever you did, keep doing it."

"Netta Vire. Carries our books between here and the crossing, and the roads have gotten unfriendly to people who carry things." He nods past you. "Walk her to Wren at the post. Nothing more complicated than that."
"She still needs both legs and the ledger under her arm. Go on."
"Wren tells me she arrived talking your ear off. Good work regardless."

"Corran Vess. Kept our books for two years and kept a second set for himself." The chalk stops for the first time. "He's gone to ground past the ruin wall east of here. What happens when you find him is your call, not mine."
"Someone closed that account already." He does not ask who. "Word travels. It doesn't need to travel through me."
"Dead, run off, or talked into paying back what he owes — I'm told all three settle the ledger. I only care that it's settled."
"East past the ruin wall. Try not to make it my business twice."
"Still owes us, last I checked. Go settle it."
"Settled is settled. I stopped asking how, and you'd do well to stop offering."
He is leaning on the Ledger House's wall with his arms crossed, watching the street the way a man watches something he has already decided about.
"Made it in, then." He looks you over once, unhurried. "Grieve's work is honest work, which is more than the word usually means around here. Do it enough times and it stops being a favour."
"Ledger House business." He does not move from the wall. "If you're not on the roster, you're on the street."
How long have you been in?
He is sitting with his back to the ruin wall, a strongbox within reach and no weapon drawn. He watches you the way a man watches a debt arrive.
"Took them long enough." He does not reach for the box. "Two years of their coin and I kept a fifth for myself. Call it a fee for the counting. I'll not pretend it was owed to me."
"That's more mercy than the ledger extends most men." He is already gathering the box. "I won't be found twice. Tell them whatever settles it for you."
She keeps both hands on the ledger case, watching the road behind you more than she watches you.
"The post. Wren's post." She lets a breath out she had clearly been keeping. "I can carry my own case from here."
Dallow Grieve pays by the head for bandits working the roads the Iron Syndicate protects. No proof required, no questions asked — just fewer bandits.
Netta Vire carries the Syndicate's books between Hollowreach and the Crossway, and the roads have gotten unfriendly to people who carry things. Walk her to Wren at the mercenary post.
Escort Netta Vire to the Crossway post

Corran Vess skimmed two years off the Syndicate's books and has gone to ground east of the Ledger House. What happens when you find him is yours to decide — the Syndicate only wants the account closed.
A bookkeeper who skimmed what he counted and ran before the tally caught up with him. No soldier and no bandit — cornered, not dangerous by trade.
What would you have me bring you?
I found what you asked for.

"There's a copy of the Treatise on Wardings loose in the market — Tam Quillfellow's Scriptorium has it on a shelf where anyone with the coin can read what we meant to keep close. Ask him about it. Then come back and tell me what you learned, and I'll know whether you can be trusted with the rest of this room."
"The Scriptorium is in the market. He'll talk, if you ask the right way."
"Go on, then. I'm not going anywhere."
"So. You went, you asked, and you came back instead of keeping it to yourself — that's the whole test, and you've passed it."
"Welcome to the Veiled Archive. Admission is granted once, and I've just granted it — mind you don't make me regret the exception."
You asked me to look into the Ancient.
"I did. Tell me plainly — did it teach you, or did you take what it had?"
It taught me. I never raised a hand to it.
It's dead. I read what the hoard kept.
"Either way, the word is recovered and the Archive is richer for it. You've earned your rank — wear it quietly, the way we do everything else."

"The waystone in the Ember Crown's town square, and the one at the Frostfang clan hold — stand at both and tell me what the Weave feels like at each. I have the books; I don't have the legs, or the reasons the Keeper won't spare to send me herself."
I'll walk both and report back.
"Start wherever's closer. The ley line doesn't care which end you read first."
"Fair enough. The stones aren't going anywhere either."
"Still waiting on your legs, not my books."
You said there was a thing to go and settle.

"The Ancient in the Frostfang aerie is the nearest thing this realm has to a living book. Go and see it — spare it or don't, that's yours to decide — and bring the Keeper whatever you come back knowing. She'll want to hear it from someone who was there."
"Mind yourself up there. It hasn't killed a visitor yet, but there's a first time in everything."
"It'll keep. It's been keeping for longer than either of us."
"No word from the aerie yet, then."
Keeper Ysolde Marr won't take you on faith. Ask Tam Quillfellow at the Scriptorium about the loose copy of the Treatise on Wardings, then bring her what you learn.
Ask Tam Quillfellow about the Treatise on Wardings
Tell Keeper Ysolde Marr what you learned
Two Ends of the Same Line
Ferris Vail wants the ley line under the market settled, once and for all. Stand at the Ember Crown waystone and at the Frostfang waystone, and tell him what the Weave feels like at each.
Read the Weave at the Ember Crown waystone
Read the Weave at the Frostfang waystone
Tell Ferris Vail what you felt at both stones
The Ancient in the Frostfang aerie holds knowledge older than the Archive itself. Go to it, spare it or don't, and bring Keeper Ysolde Marr whatever you come back knowing.
Tell Keeper Ysolde Marr what the Ancient taught you
Tell Keeper Ysolde Marr what the hoard kept
The lightning-rod stands dead. While the Iron King still rules the Crown, the storm will not answer you.

Where the Third Flamebearer fell, the air still hums. His hatred had a centre, and it is lying in the snow, crackling. It would make you fast, and cruel, and very hard to stop. Will you absorb the flame?
Let the storm die with him.
Thunder rolls through you and does not stop. For a moment you understand him completely: how good it felt to break things that had stopped deserving mercy.
You close your fist around the shard and refuse it. The static drains out of the sky, and for the first time in an age the Stormcrown is quiet.

keys: # --- Finish run: the endings and credits ---

en: You set the relics down around the empty throne and do not sit.
The fire in them does not go out. It goes home: into the ground, the rivers, the thin grey sky. The Weave draws a long breath for the first time in an age.

In the years after, the ash stops falling. Green comes back to the Crown's fields and the wind off Frostfang carries rain instead of cinders. One spring, a dragon is seen over the Stormcrown, and nobody runs.
There are no more Flamebearers. There does not need to be. The Age of Ash ends, and the Age of Dawn begins.
You carried none of the fallen into that hall. The songs call you the Unburnt, and for once the songs are right.
You carried some of the fallen with you, and it cost you. Some nights the old fire still wakes in your hands. You let it gutter, every time.
You took every ember and still walked away from the throne. No one who saw you do it has ever been able to explain how.
Morthul's ash settles. The throne is warm, and it has been waiting a very long time. You sit.
Every ember you carried roars up to meet it. The sky over Embervale stops dying, because you tell it to.
The monsters kneel. The roads are safe. The harvests come in on time, every time, exactly as you have decreed. No one argues, because no one can.
The world survives. Freedom does not. The Age of Ash ends, and the Age of Embers begins.
You came to the throne with clean hands and took it anyway. The fallen would have understood that better than anyone.
The embers you took whisper that you are not like the others who fell. For a thousand years, you believe them.
Six fallen Flamebearers burn inside you now, and the seventh sits above them all. The old names are forgotten. There is only yours.
Made with Godot. Characters generated with Meshy. World built from Quaternius's CC0 kits.
Thank you for playing. The world remains yours to walk.
The Third Flamebearer. Hatred was the fire he was given and the only one he kept. He climbed the Stormcrown to be closer to the lightning, and it has been answering him ever since.

keys: # The Ashen Wilds (2026-09 finish run): the Beast Lord
en: Last Hearth and the Ash Hunters' station.

The Fourth Flamebearer. He was given the ember to save the world, and when the Cataclysm broke it he stopped pretending the world was his to save. He took the corruption in whole, and what is left of him leads the things that live in the scar.
Light the blighted brazier and call the Beast Lord
The brazier will not take. Something is still asleep on the plateau.
Where the Beast Lord fell, the ember still beats inside the ash of him, quick and hungry, like something that wants to run. It is yours to take. Will you absorb the flame?
It goes into you like a pulse. Your senses sharpen past comfort, and for a moment every living thing on the plateau is only meat and distance. The bargain is struck.
You step back from it. The ember gutters in the ash, and the Wilds go quiet, the way a forest goes quiet when the hunter has gone.

She looks you over the way you would look over a cart come in off a bad road. "You came through the Breach on purpose. Nobody does that. Sit by the fire if you like; it is the only thing here we do not ration."

"Last Hearth. We named it the first winter, when it was a joke. There were forty of us came over when the Breach was still open, looking for kin and salvage. There are eleven now. The houses were here before us. Whoever built them did not need roofs, or did not live long enough to want them."

"The Hunters keep a station on the rise, north and east. Past that the road climbs to a plateau under the wall, and on the plateau there is something that used to be a man. The beasts go to him. So do our dead, some nights, and we do not go after them."
She is quiet a long time. "Then the wolves will stop coming to the fence in threes. I will believe it when I have slept a night through. Thank you. I do not know what else a person says."
She does not look up from the bandage she is winding. "If you are bleeding, sit. If you are not, mind where you stand; the ash gets into everything, and into wounds first."
I will leave you to it.

"Nothing, at first. Then a cut does not close, and the skin round it goes grey, and the one who has it starts to hear the wolves as if they were talking. I burn what I can. I have not found anything else that works."
A lean man in an ash-grey tabard, sighting down the road with his hand over his eyes. "Hunter, or lost? Either way you walked a long way to stand on my rise."
Tell me about the Beast Lord.
What are the Hunters doing out here?

"He was one of the Flamebearers, if you believe the old songs, and I do. When the fire went wrong he did not fight it. He let it in and let it make him what it wanted. Now he sleeps on the plateau until something wakes him, and every beast in the scar knows where he is. There is a brazier at the head of the ramp. Light it and he comes. Do not light it unless you mean it."

"Watching. The Guild wants to know what comes out of the scar before it reaches the Breach. We count the packs, we mark the corrupted ones, and we keep the Hearth folk alive when we can. It is not glorious. It is the job."

He lowers his hand from his eyes. "I saw the fire go out from here. The packs are scattering: no one calling them any more. The Guild will want your name for the ledger, whether you want it there or not."
A short man behind a stall built out of three different doors. "Everything here came out of a ruin or off a body, and I will not tell you which. You buying, or selling?"
"I go out at dawn, when the beasts are sleeping it off. Houses, carts, the dead. The Breach used to bring traders. Now it brings you. You will do."
"Counter is shut. Nothing good happens in the scar after dark, and I am not staying up to find out what I would be selling to."
Where does all this come from?
I will leave you to it.

keys: # Sunspire Dominion — the realm south of the Southmarch Gate: Saffra Wells

en: The Fifth Flamebearer. He listened for the gods after they fell silent, and something answered. He became its voice, and built an empire of worshippers to carry what it said. He does not preach Morthul's word. He preaches in it.
Kindle the altar fire and call the Prophet
The altar fire will not take. The Prophet is not ready to hear you.
Where the Prophet fell, his fire keeps speaking: a low, patient voice that knows your name and has been waiting to say it. The ember is yours to take. Will you absorb the flame?
The voice comes into you with the heat. For a moment you understand every sermon he ever gave, and for a moment you agree.
You close your hand on nothing. The voice goes on a while without you, and then the sanctum is only a room full of smoke.

"Mind the sand on the stair. It comes in on every boot and it has been coming in for four hundred years." She does not look up from the page. "This is the great library, or what the desert left of it. The Veiled Archive keeps it now."

"The last reading hall of the city that stood here before the Cataclysm. The rest of it is under your feet. The mesa kept the wind off this one hall, so it kept its books. Some of what we know about the Flamebearers, we know only because of that wind."
Tell me about the Crimson Prophet.

"He was one of the seven, once. He read in this hall. Then he began to hear an answer when he prayed, and he stopped reading. His mission is south, past the red flats. His worshippers walk the pilgrim track every day."
"Caravan master, for what that's worth this season. The wells take anyone with coin, and the cots are ten a night. Don't drink from the oasis upstream of the cattle."
"West to the library, if you like old books and older sand. South to the Crimson Mission, if you like sermons. My caravans go neither way. We turn round here and go home."
"The Iron King sealed it. His wardens would not let a cart through in either direction. Now he's gone and the road's open, and I've got twenty years of trade to make up."
Then I'll leave you to it.
"Water's free. Everything else at the wells costs something, but not the water. That's the oldest law in the Dominion and the Prophet's people can preach at me all they like."
"Every week, in their red, asking who will walk south with them. Some go. They come back quieter, when they come back. My grandson went at midsummer."
"I walked the pilgrim track twice. I'm not walking it a third time. Don't tell the ones in red I said so."

"He speaks from the sanctum with the altar fire behind him, and the fire speaks with him. Everyone hears their own name in it. The faithful stand at the walls. If you mean to go in there, go in armed, and do not light the altar unless you mean it."

keys: # Finish run: the hidden realm and the Hollow Queen. Post-reveal text only
en: keyed pale.* (tools/world_atlas.py exempts that prefix); nothing outside pale.* may name the realm.
The Second Flamebearer. She sought immortality and lost her soul for it. She hid a whole kingdom from death, and then from history, and commands the dead who were not so lucky.
Light the brazier and ask for an audience
The brazier will not take a flame.

Where she fell the air is still and very cold, and at its centre a fragment of fallen divinity waits without beating. It offers what it offered her: to keep you exactly as you are, forever. Will you absorb the flame?
The cold goes into you like a held breath. Something in you stops, very quietly, and does not start again. The bargain is struck.
You leave it where it lies. Behind you, for the first time in four hundred years, the light begins to move.

A visitor. There has not been a visitor since the day of signing. You will forgive me if I read you the proclamation; I read it to everyone, and there has not been anyone. "By the Queen's grace the Concord is kept, and none within it shall fail." It is still evening. It is always still evening.

The world was ending. You know that part, surely, out there. She offered us an exemption, and we signed, all of us, the whole kingdom in one hand. Nobody dies here. Nobody leaves. Nobody is born. We keep the city in repair because repair is something to do.

She is in the Hollow Court at the end of the processional way. She preserved us, and then she preserved herself, and then there was nothing left in her to preserve. Her servants walk the roads. They are not us. We were never buried.
The light moved. Did you see it? For the first time in four hundred years the light moved. I have no proclamation for this. I think I shall sit down.
Mind the flame. They never go out, you understand. I light them anyway. A lamplighter who does not light lamps is only a man standing in the street at dusk, and there are enough of those.

I signed with the rest. I remember the ink was cold. I thought: I will never have to watch my daughter grow old. I have not. She has not grown at all. That was the price, and we paid it in the wrong coin.
Past the fields, up the processional. Do not go if you mean to bargain with her. Everything here is something she was once offered in trade.
My hand is tired. My hand has not been tired in four hundred years. I believe I will let the lamps go out tonight, and see what it is like.
Bread? It is fresh. It has been fresh since the day she signed us. Nobody eats it. Nobody needs to. I bake it because the ovens are warm and my hands remember how.
Nothing ripens here and nothing rots. You would think that was a mercy. It is only a very long afternoon. Most of us stopped wanting the exemption a long time ago. We cannot hand it back.
Her people come for nothing and take nothing. They are the dead she commands, from outside. We are the ones she kept. There is a difference, and it is the only thing we still own.
The loaves have gone stale. Can you smell it? Stale bread. I could weep. I think I shall bake one more, and eat it myself.

Look at the dial. Five and twenty past five. It has said five and twenty past five for four hundred years, and every day I wind it, because a clock that is not wound is a lie, and a clock that does not move is only a mistake.
She wrote us out of every map and every history. That was the last of it: the secret. If nobody knows we are here, nobody can come to tell us what we have missed. And yet here you are.
Her Court is north. The ring before it was built for audiences. Light the brazier and she will give you one. She has not refused an audience in four hundred years. She has not had one.
The hand moved. Six o'clock. I have waited all my life, and then all of the rest of it, to say that it is six o'clock.

column4: the braziers and the throne placeholder.

en: The Sixth Flamebearer, and the closest any of them came. He reached the Ash Throne, raised his blade over Morthul and did not bring it down. Whatever he saw in that moment, he has served the god of endings ever since, and he waits at the last gate for the one who might finish what he could not.

The god of entropy, who looked at creation and judged that everything ends, even gods, and so everything should. He killed the six who stood against him and has sat in their ruined heaven ever since, while the world he broke goes on dying.
Light the brazier and face the Ashen Knight
Light the last fire and challenge the Ash King
The fire will not wake while the Knight still holds the gate.
He goes down on one knee and plants the greatsword so he does not fall further. "Good. Good. I was beginning to think there would never be anyone."
Why did you stop, at the throne?

"Because I saw what sits in it. Not a god. A chair that must never be empty. I could kill him, or I could become him, and I could not choose. So I knelt. Choose better than I did, Seventh. Take my ember or leave it in the ash, but do not kneel."
His ember gutters in the cracked breastplate, grey and heavy, the strongest fire of the six. It is yours to take. Will you absorb the flame?
His strength pours into you, disciplined and vast, and with it the memory of a blade held still above a throne. The bargain is struck.
You leave the ember where it lies. It burns down slowly beside him, and for the first time since the Cataclysm the Ashen Knight is at rest.

The Iron King was the first of the fallen, not the last. Three more Flamebearers hold the known realms: the Storm Tyrant in Frostfang's high passes, the Beast Lord somewhere in the Ashen Wilds beyond the Breach, and the Crimson Prophet who rules Sunspire from his temple. End them, and decide what to do with what burns inside each.
Defeat the Storm Tyrant at the Stormcrown
Defeat the Beast Lord in the Ashen Wilds
Defeat the Crimson Prophet in Sunspire

With three of the fallen gone, the embers you carry pull west, towards a place no map admits exists. The Archivist of the Sunspire library says a door beneath her stacks has begun to open. There were seven Flamebearers. You have only met five.
Find the Second Flamebearer and end her reign

Every fallen Flamebearer died saying the same thing in a different way: that you do not understand what you are for. The Archivist in the Sunspire library has kept the gods' own records. It is time to read them.
Hear the truth from the Archivist in the Sunspire library
The way to the ruined Celestial Realm stands open in the library. Morthul waits on the Ash Throne, and between you and him stands the Sixth Flamebearer, the one who came closest.
Confront Morthul at the Ash Throne

The fallen hold the realms you can find on a map. There were seven of you, and the Second hid her country from death itself. When the Tyrant, the Beast and the Prophet are gone, her door will stop hiding from you. It opens here, under my floor. I have been listening to it breathe for forty years.
Tell me the truth. All of it.

Seven gods kept the world. Morthul was the one who kept its endings: death, rot, the last page. One day he decided the whole book was flawed and should be burned so it could be written again. The others refused. The war that followed broke the continents. Six gods died. He did not.

Here is what the songs leave out. Morthul is not a tyrant who took a throne. He is what the throne makes of whoever sits on it. Something must hold the world's endings, or nothing ends at all and nothing can begin. He sat because someone had to. It hollowed him into the Ash King.
