The gods made seven Flamebearers to unseat him. Not one of them was ever told the rest: that when he falls, the throne will ask for you. The fallen all heard it, in the end. Some ran from it. Some said yes too early. You carry their fire. What you do with it at the top of the Celestial stair is the only choice that has ever mattered.
Open the way to the Celestial Realm.
Then go. The stair is behind the last shelf; it has always been there, waiting for someone who knew what it was. Whatever you choose up there, Seventh, choose it awake.
It is open. It will stay open. I am not going to talk you out of it, and I am not going to talk you into it.

Morthul comes apart into ash, and the ash does not settle. It waits. The Ash Throne stands empty for the first time since the gods died, and you feel it the way you felt every ember you ever held: a question. Someone must always sit here.
Refuse it. Give the fire back to the world.

If you refuse, the relics you carry spill their fire back into the land, and nothing holds the world's endings but the world itself. It will be slower. It will be free. It will be yours no longer. Is this your choice?
Yes. Let the world keep its own endings.
If you sit, every ember you carry becomes a crown. You will end the dying because you order it to end, and nothing in Embervale will ever again be able to tell you no. Is this your choice?
Yes. The world will survive, because I will make it.
The Ash Throne. It is carved from something that was once alive, and it is never empty for long.
Step back. He still sits there.
Not yet. I need a moment.
A VISION. A young soldier kneels in the rain before six dying gods, and the first fire of the world is put into his hands.
He wins his first war with it. Then his second. Every victory needs a little more of the fire, and a little more obedience from everyone around him.
By the end he is not fighting Morthul at all. He is building walls around a crown, and calling it keeping the world safe.
A VISION. The Third Flamebearer comes home from the Celestial stair to find his clan hold burned by men who swore they were saving it.
He calls the storm down on them. It answers so gladly that he never quite lets it go again.
He climbs the Stormcrown to be alone with the only thing that has never lied to him: the lightning, and the hatred it carries.
A VISION. The Fourth Flamebearer walks into the Ashen Wilds to cure the corruption at its root, alone, because she will not ask anyone else to risk it.
The rot does not fight her. It offers. Strength that never tires, senses that never sleep. Only a little of her, at first.
The last of her that could say no is buried under antler and fur and hunger. The Wilds remember her name. The beast does not.
A VISION. The Fifth Flamebearer reads in the great library for thirty years, looking for a way to win that does not cost the world.
One night a voice answers his prayers. It is patient, and kind, and it tells him that endings are a mercy.
He does not think he betrayed anyone. He thinks he found the truth first, and he has been building a church to share it ever since.
A VISION. The Second Flamebearer watches her whole realm age while the war drags on, and cannot bear to lose one more of them.
She takes her people out of time. No one dies. No one grows. The evening simply never ends.
The price was her own soul, and she paid it without looking. She has been counting her people every dusk for four hundred years.
A VISION. The Sixth Flamebearer climbs the Celestial stair with five companions. He is the only one who reaches the top.
He stands before the Ash Throne with Morthul broken at his feet, and hears what the throne asks of whoever wins.
He could not sit, and he could not leave it empty. So he knelt, and has guarded the one who would, ever since. He was waiting for you.
Huntmaster Yrsa Kesk's counts from the Ashen Wilds no longer add up. Stand on Hask Morrow's rise above the scar road, hear his count, and see the ash-maws for yourself.
Reach the Ash Hunters' station in the Ashen Wilds

The Hunters' ledger calls every dragon the same thing. Look at the wild drakes, the ash-drakes and the Ancient in Frostfang Reach, from as close as you dare, then tell Yrsa Kesk what the ledger should say about each.
Observe the wild drakes at the Dragon Roost
Observe the ash-drakes at the Ash Roost
Observe the Ancient at its Aerie
Is there work for a marked hunter?
The Ashen count is still open.
I've been to the scar. Hask's count is right.
I carry the mark. I'll go.
I haven't seen all three yet.
Here's what the ledger should say.
Mark them all. Fire is fire, and all of it burns.
Hunt the ash-drakes. Leave the wild ones. Protect the one that speaks.
Pull the Hunters out of dragon country. We don't know enough.

She finds a page near the back of the field book. "Hask Morrow keeps our station in the Ashen Wilds, on the rise above the scar road. He sends me pack counts, and lately they don't add up. Once you carry the Tracker's mark, go and stand on his rise, hear his count, and put down three ash-maws yourself. Then tell me what you saw, not what you killed."
"Last Hearth is the only fire on that road. The station is on the rise above it. Write things down."
"Then it's still open. Hask won't have gone anywhere. Neither have the maws."
She turns the book so you can see your name in it, twice now. "Right, and worse than he said. You carry the Hunter's mark. Hunters who carry it get the questions the rest of us can't answer yet."

"Dragons." She says it flatly. "The ledger calls them all one thing and they are not. There are wild drakes at the Dragon Roost in the Reach, ash-drakes the ember got into at the Ash Roost, and the old one at the Aerie that talks. Go and look at all three, from as close as you dare and no closer. Then tell me what the Hunters should do about each. Whatever you say goes in the ledger, and the ledger outlives both of us."
"From cover, if you can. A dragon you watched is worth ten you fought."
"Then you haven't seen dragons yet. Only a dragon."
She opens the book at a clean page and holds the pen over it. "Go on."
"One line for each of them, or one line for all of them. Your choice, and it stands."
The pen moves. "Every dragon a mark. It's simple, and simple travels well. It will cost us hunters. It always does."
"Every dragon a mark, and the marks are coming in. So are the names of the hunters who didn't come back. I read both lists."

The pen moves slowly, three lines instead of one. "The ember is in the ash-drakes and not in the others. And a creature that can tell you why it's angry isn't game." She blots the page. "That's a harder ledger to keep. It's the right one."
"Two ash-drakes marked since you left, and the wild roost untouched. The old one at the Aerie watched our hunters pass and let them. I think it knows what we decided."

The pen hesitates, then moves. "Knowing when we don't know. Most orders never learn it." She draws a line across the Reach on her map. "The station at the scar stays. The roosts are closed to us until someone knows more than you do."
"The roosts are quiet, or we don't know otherwise, which is what we chose. Hask still counts the scar. That was always the job."

She closes the book on the page and keeps her hand on it. "Then hear mine. You hunted with your eyes before your bow, all the way to the dragons. That is the Ashbane's mark, and it is the last one we give."
"The Tally in your pack has a knot for every dragon this lodge ever judged. Yours is the newest. Wear it where people can see it."

He doesn't take his eyes off the road. "Forty-one maws past the rise since the thaw, and nine of them wrong in the way the ember makes them wrong. Last year it was twelve and two. Tell her the numbers. Tell her I'm not guessing."
"Ashbane, is it? Word travels up this road slower than ash, but it travels." He almost smiles. "The station's yours whenever you want a roof. Same rule as everyone: write it down."
Something is eating the bindings in the great library's lower stacks. Walk the library in the Sunspire Dominion and clear the ruin crawlers out of the sand around it.
Reach the great library in the Sunspire Dominion

What the Breach did to the people near it survives in three places: the Breach stones, the survivors at Last Hearth, and a poor copy in the great library. Gather all three for Keeper Ysolde Marr, then decide what the Archive does with them.
Take rubbings of the stones at the Ashen Breach
Hear the survivors' account at Last Hearth
Set the record beside the great library's copy
Is there more work for a member?
The crawlers are still at the stacks.
What aren't you sure you should keep?
I have the whole Breach record.
Here is what the Archive should do.
How does the Breach record fare?
Keep it here, veiled, for the few who need it.
Copy it out. The people at the Hearth and the Wells deserve to know.
Seal it. Some knowledge only teaches people how to repeat it.

"There is a greater house than this Annexe: the great library in the Sunspire Dominion, half under the sand. Something has got into its lower stacks and is eating the bindings." Her hands stay behind her back. "Readers may go and deal with it. Walk the library, put down the crawlers in the sand around it, and come back. The work is dull. Most of our work is."
"Take the caravan road south through the Southmarch Gate. The library is beyond Saffra Wells. Mind the sand."
"Then so is the damage. Go on."

"The greater house is grateful in the way houses are: silently, and for a very long time." Her hands come apart. "You are an Archivist of this house. What comes to an Archivist is what we are not sure we should keep."

"The Breach record. What the Breach did to the people standing near it. It is cut into the stones at the Breach itself, remembered by the survivors at Last Hearth, and copied once, badly, into a book in the great library. Gather all three. Then decide what the Archive does with it. I will not decide for you. That is what the rank is for."
"The stones first, while they still read. Then the Hearth. Then the library, to set it beside the copy."
"Incomplete is the natural state of a record. Finish it anyway."
She takes the rubbings and your notes and lays them side by side on the sill without reading them. "Before I read a word: what happens to it?"
"Keep it veiled, give it away, or put it where no one reads it again. Those are the only three things an archive can do with anything."
"The oldest answer, and the one we are named for." She slides the record into a case and turns the key. "It will be here, for whoever needs it and can say why."
"Veiled, and read twice this season, both times by members who could say why. That is the system working."

For a moment she looks as though she will argue. "Copied out, it stops being ours. It stops being anyone's." She reaches for fresh paper anyway. "Coran will make the copies and the caravans will carry them. The Archive will learn what it is to be read."
"Coran's copies reached the Wells and the Hearth. A caravan master wrote to ask what else we have. I did not know what to say to that. I am learning."

"Sealed." She says it without relief. "Not burned. We do not burn. But it goes into the vault under the Annexe, and the vault does not open for anyone who asks politely." She wraps the rubbings in waxed cloth.
"Sealed, and no one has asked for it. Which means either we were right, or no one knows it is gone. I think about the second more than I would like."
"Then it is the Archive's decision, and you made it. Very few members are ever asked. Fewer answer." Her hands go behind her back again. "You are Keeper of the Veil, the last rank we have."
"The seal ring in your pack is the custodian's. It opens every case in this room and in the great library too. Try not to need it."
The Keeper says I hold the Veil now.
"Then you may sign for anything in this room." He slides the ledger across, pen and all. "Nobody ever does. It is a comfort to know someone could."
Idrys Vane's caravans are losing guards to red-robed raiders between the Caravan Gap and Saffra Wells. Walk the road for the Ledger House and make it stop.

A Citadel factor is paying the Ledger House to lift Idrys Vane's route ledger from the Caravanserai. Rook Sallow is already on the job. Get the ledger, speak with Rook, and bring Broker Ilder Vance an ending.
Take Vane's route ledger at the Caravanserai
Speak with Rook Sallow at the Ledger House
Any contracts for someone with a rank?
The road contract is still open.
I'm a Runner. I'll take it.
I have Vane's ledger, and I've spoken to Rook.
How did the Southmarch business settle?
The contract as written. The factor gets the ledger.
Vane paid better. The ledger goes back to him, and the House takes its cut.
Whatever happens to the ledger, Rook walks free of it.

"The Southmarch road is open again, and Idrys Vane's caravans are the first on it. Men in red robes have been lifting his guards between the Caravan Gap and Saffra Wells. Vane pays the Ledger House to make that stop." He taps the contract. "Ranked hands only. Runners and up. Walk the road from the Gap to the Wells and put three of the robes in the sand."
"Vane is at the wells. He pays on delivery and not a coin before."
"Open contracts are unpaid contracts. Close it."

"Vane paid in full and asked for you by name, which is the most expensive thing a client can do." He folds a contract and keeps it. "You're a Contractor of this House. Contractors get the work that comes with somebody else's interest attached."

"A factor out of the Citadel wants Vane's caravans broken, now that he has proved they run. He is paying us to take Vane's route ledger out of the Caravanserai, quietly. Rook Sallow is already on it. Get the ledger, see Rook, and bring me an ending. What kind of ending is yours to choose. I only need it clean."
"The Caravanserai at the wells. Rook knows the rest. Rook always knows the rest."
"Then it's the only thing in this district that isn't. Finish it."

He doesn't reach for the ledger. "Vane offered you more to lose it. The factor offered me more to get it. And Rook has been on the factor's payroll longer than he's been on mine." He almost smiles. "So. What did we sell?"
"Say it plainly. The Ledger House writes it down the way you say it."
"Terms, payment, and the ending everyone agreed to." He takes the ledger at last. "Vane will hate us. The Citadel will hire us again. That is what fidelity costs and what it buys."
"The factor's caravans run the road now and Vane runs what's left. Nobody in Saffra Wells will pour you a drink. Everybody in the Citadel will."

"A better offer, taken openly, with the House's share on the table." He weighs the ledger and hands it back. "The creed is terms and payment. Nobody ever said whose. Vane will remember it. So will the factor."
"Vane's caravans still run, and every season he sends a crate of dates with a note that says 'for the cut'. The factor has hired elsewhere. Elsewhere is cheaper and worse."

He looks at you for a long moment. "You sold the contract to keep a man who was selling us." A pause. "The Syndicate is loyal to the contract, never the cause. You found a third thing to be loyal to. I'll allow it once."
"Rook works the wall outside, and he works it for us now. He owes you, he knows it, and he hates knowing it. That makes him the most reliable man I have."

"Written." And he does, for once, in a small book from his coat. "Three rungs, and you've stood on every one. You're Ironhand. There is no rung above it, only the Broker's chair, and I'm sitting in it."
"The signet in your pack opens doors from Hollowreach to the Wells. Every fence and factor on the road knows it. Use it like a contract: carefully, and in writing."
The Broker says you're on the Citadel job.
You know I wear a Dawnwarden's rank too.

He doesn't move off the wall. "I'm on the Citadel's payroll, if that's what he's too polite to say. Two winters now. The factor pays me to know what the House does before it does it." He finally looks at you. "Tell Vance or don't. I'll know which by morning."

"A Dawnblade and a Syndicate contract in the same coat." He snorts. "The Watch would call that a conflict. The House calls it a wider client list. Keep the two ledgers apart and nobody here will care."
The Ledger House sends its regards.
"The Ledger House, is it." He looks at the signet before he looks at you. "Whatever the Syndicate decided about my road, it decided it with your hands. I'll remember the hands."
Hierarch Selane Ott sends the Kindled to see what a Flamebearer leaves behind. Visit Stormcrown in the high passes of Frostfang Reach, then hear Warder Cass Vollen on custody.
Visit Stormcrown in the high passes of Frostfang Reach
Hear Warder Cass Vollen on custody
The Emberbound have never agreed on what they are for. See a beast the ember remade at the Ash Roost, read the order's founding doctrine in the great library, then give the Hierarch your answer.
See the ash-drakes at the Ash Roost
Read the founding doctrine in the great library
Is there more to learn down here?
I've seen Stormcrown, and heard Cass on custody.
What has the order argued about?
I've seen the roost and read the doctrine.
I'll go and see, and read.
How does the order hold to the doctrine?
Safeguard them. Keep every relic warded until no one needs it.
Destroy them. Whatever can be broken should be.
Use them. We understand the fire better than anyone. Carry it.

"There is more to learn everywhere the fire has been. Stormcrown, in the high passes of the Reach: the Tyrant stood there long enough to change the stone." The lamp comes up a little. "The Kindled may go and see what a Flamebearer leaves behind. Then ask Cass what we do with what's left. He'll tell you. He tells everyone."
"Go armed. The stone remembers more than the storm does."

"Then you've seen what the fire leaves and heard what we do with it." The lamp comes up. "You're Ember-Sworn now. The Ember-Sworn are told the thing this order has argued about since before it had a name."

"What we are for. Some of us say we keep the relics safe until no one needs them. Some say we should break them, if they can be broken. Some say they're tools and we're cowards not to use them." She sets the lamp down. "Go and see an ash-drake at its roost, a living thing the ember remade. Then read our founding doctrine. It's shelved in the great library in the Sunspire, under a title nobody would take down. Then come back and tell me which of us is right."
"The Ash Roost in the Reach first. The library after. Read it slowly."
"Then you know as much as I did when I had to choose." She doesn't sit. "The order will follow whatever its chosen voice says. Tonight, that's you."
"You kept it, and you're still yourself. That counts as evidence. For which side, I don't know yet. Say it."
I gave up what I carried.
"You gave it up before anyone asked twice. That counts as evidence. For which side, I don't know yet. Say it."
"Before you give it: I remember what you told me at the foot of the stair."
"Custody." She nods slowly. "Cass will be pleased and won't show it. The order stays what it has been: a list, a ward, and a long wait."
"Cass has three new names on his list and nothing has left the pedestal. It is a slow kind of winning. It is still winning."

"Then we become the people who break what we don't understand." She says it without scorn. "It might be the only honest answer. Bren will start asking what breaks an ember. I hope he finds out slowly."
"Bren broke a lesser relic at the bottom of the cut. It took a day and cost him his eyebrows, and the ember went out. So we can. We are less sure we should have learned that."
The lamp flares, briefly, as though something heard. "Then we stop studying the fire and start carrying it." For a moment her look is almost afraid. "It begins with whoever said it. Hold still."
Heat runs up your arm and settles behind your eyes, and does not leave. "There," she says quietly. "Now you know what we're asking of everyone else."
"Two of ours carry the fire now, the way you do. They are stronger and they are quieter, and I watch both of them. Someone should be watching you too. It may as well be me."
"Then it's the order's doctrine, and it was your voice that said it." She takes the lamp up. "Kindled, Ember-Sworn, and now Flamekeeper. It's the last thing we call anyone."
"Cass warded the ashglass in your pack himself. It won't stop the fire. It will tell you when the fire is close."
The Hierarch sent me to hear about custody.

"Custody." He says it like a prayer he has stopped believing and kept saying. "Every relic gets a line: where it came from, who carried it, what it did to them. The line is the ward. A relic nobody has written down is a relic somebody is using." He taps the pedestal. "That's all custody is. It's enough."
"So I heard." He does not step aside, but for the first time he turns his back on you to face the pedestal. "Then you're on the list now too. Everyone who decides what we're for ends up on it."

keys: # Phase 44.5 + 47.5 (finishing features): the Ashen Knight's rival duels and the world after the ending

en: A brazier of black iron, cold, ringed with a knight's sigil drawn in ash. Someone is waiting for the storm to break.
A brazier of black iron, cold, ringed with a knight's sigil drawn in ash. Someone is waiting for the Prophet to fall.
He steps back and lowers the greatsword, breathing hard behind a visor black with old fire. "Enough. The Tyrant fell to you, so I came to see what kind of thing could fell him."
"I was the Sixth to carry the flame, and the nearest any of us came to the end of it. Now I keep a stair you have not climbed yet."
"Because you are not ready, and I would rather meet you when you are. Gather your embers, Seventh. We will cross blades again." He turns into the storm and is gone.
This time he yields a step at a time, and he is smiling behind the visor; you can hear it. "Better. Much better. The Prophet burned for his certainty, and you did not flinch from the fire."
"I keep measuring you. Every ember you take brings you a little closer to where I stand."
"At the top of a stair, before a throne, with a choice I could not make. Come when you are ready. I will not yield a third time."
At the Stormcrown, you let me live.
"I did. I needed to know whether you would keep climbing. You did."
In the Mission, you yielded a second time.
"And I told you I would not yield a third. I kept my word. So did you."
How is the village, now it is over?
"The forge has not gone cold since. The children count the clear mornings out loud, as if they might run out. I stopped looking north. There is nothing there to dread any more."

He will not meet your eyes. "The village keeps your fires burning, as you commanded. We have learned the new prayers. Please, the sky has been red for so long. Is there anything more you require of us?"
"We stopped rationing the firewood. First winter in living memory. Someone planted beans by the fence, and the wolves only come to look at them."
"We do as we are told, and the ash falls, and we sweep it. The hearth burns for you now. Everyone knows whose fire it is." She says it very carefully.
"Deeper and sweeter every season. The caravans sing coming in, now. Water is still free. Some laws are worth keeping."
"The water runs warm and tastes of smoke. Your priests come to bless it every dusk, and nobody drinks until they have gone." She lowers her voice. "It is still free. Please do not change that."

keys: # --- magic-core: this group's keys go between the markers (one owner per block); prefix magic.cast.* ---

en: Marked by fire. The third Kindle in a row detonates in a burst that ignites everything it touches.
Burns for a few seconds. Stacks make it hurt more.
Slowed by the cold. A frost hit on a chilled foe freezes it.
Frozen solid: cannot move or act for a moment, and brittle. Then immune to freezing for a while.
Held fast by thorns. Cannot move on foot but can still act.
Cannot cast. A cast in its wind-up is broken.
Every lightning hit nearby arcs to this mark.
Armour up, and casting cannot be interrupted by a stagger.
Takes more damage, and Necrotic lifesteal off it is doubled.
Stung over time. The swarm jumps to a nearby foe when its bearer dies.
Each kill returns mana while the echo lasts.
Cannot act or move for a moment. Immune to stuns afterwards.
Rotting flesh. Hurts over time, stacks, and Knit Bone mends more for each stack.
Absorbs a fixed amount of damage, then breaks. Unspent, it returns some mana.
Spell learned: {0}. A corrupted craft, taken knowingly.
{0} is out of reach: it needs {1}, and you are {2}.
The tome is sealed. Whatever guards it is still guarding it.
{0} feeds on the dying Weave. Interact again to take it.
The Weave here is fading. Ordinary spells: {0}% power, {1}% mana. Corrupted spells: {2}% power, {3}% mana.
Rank {0}/{1}: {2} of {3} casts to the next rank
Rank {0}: cooldowns {1}% shorter. Rank {2}: {1}% shorter again
This craft feeds on the dying Weave. Press again to take it.
Lands where you aim after {0}s. A ring on the ground shows where and when.
A wall across your aim for {0}s.
A hazard: bodies can walk into it.
Dashes {0} m along your aim, striking what you pass.
Teleports up to {0} m along your aim; a wall stops you short.
Marks the target; other spells read the mark.
Silences the target and interrupts a cast in its wind-up.
Consumes a status on the target for extra damage.
A guard does not stop it.
A stagger cannot cancel the cast.
A fast, cheap bolt of flame that leaves a Kindled stack on its target; the third stack detonates.
Hold to draw a piercing lance of fire; a fuller draw pierces more foes, hits harder and burns longer.
Raise a line of fire that burns whatever crosses it and eats arrows, but does not stop bodies.
Call a meteor down on the aim point after a short warning; a direct hit crushes a raised guard.
A quick shard of ice that chills its target; a shard into a chilled foe freezes it.
A ring of cold around you that chills everything close; anything already chilled freezes.
A lingering storm around you that slows foes and stacks chill on every pulse; you can be caught in your own.
Raise a wall of solid ice that stops bodies and projectiles until it is broken or fades.
A slow homing orb that chains to a nearby foe where it lands and prefers a Stormbranded target.
Hold to channel a beam of lightning; you are slowed and can be interrupted while it runs, and it chains to a Stormbranded foe.
Dash along your aim, striking everything you pass and stunning the last foe struck.
Brand a foe so that every lightning hit within range arcs to the brand.
A lance of unmaking that strips a benefit from its target and silences it, interrupting a caster mid wind-up.
A ward that absorbs a fixed amount of damage and breaks with a flash; an unspent ward returns a share of its mana.
Step along your aim and reappear, stopped short by a wall; a shorter jump costs less mana.
Mark the ground and, after a warning, pull every foe in the area toward its centre.
Mend your wounds at once and leave a Regrowth that keeps healing for a time.
Plant a totem that heals you over time; foes can destroy it.
Thorns erupt over an area and root every foe in it; they shrug off further control for a while.
Loose a swarm that stings its target over time and jumps to a nearby foe if the bearer dies.
Harden your skin for a few seconds, raising armour and making your casting impossible to stagger.
A corrupted lance of ash-fire that drains a foe and heals you more the lower its health; only the Marked can wield it.
Pay health for a heavy blow; if it kills, the spell returns mana.
Cleanse a Decay affliction from yourself and heal more for each stack it removed.
Mark a foe so it takes more damage; necrotic lifesteal drawn from a marked foe doubles.
Ask whether they teach any spellcraft.
Ask to be taught Mending Bloom.
Mirela wipes her hands on her apron. 'I cannot spare a tonic, but I can spare a word. Mending Bloom is a herb-wife's charm, and I will show it to anyone who means to use it kindly.'
She guides your hands through the shape twice, then makes you do it alone. It holds on the third try.
Ask to be taught Stinging Swarm.
Halda glances up from the cast. 'Wasp-wives taught me one trick for things too big to fight. I can teach you the rest of it.'
She sets a paper nest between you and a post and shows you how to shake it loose without being stung. By dusk it answers your hand.
The Huntmaster shuts her field book. 'A hunter who cannot take a hit is a hunter for a season. There is a way of holding the body the way a tree holds itself.'
She has you stand under the lodge roof's edge in the rain until you stop feeling it. Then she shows you what you were doing.
Ask to be taught Rime Shard.
Ask to be taught Frost Nova.
Vetle nods at the fire. 'The cold is a tool once you stop arguing with it. I know two ways of handing it to another. Pick one.'
He takes your hands and holds them out to the fire, then turns them over. 'Now the other way. That is all of it.'
Ask to be taught Glacial Bulwark.
Hjalvar looks you over. 'The hold has stood because a wall of ice stands when a wall of men does not. I will teach you the wall.'
He walks you out into the snow and shows you where the ice wants to rise. It rises for you on the second try.
Ask to be taught Thunder Step.
Halvar turns his stump to the fire. 'I lost this hand keeping up with the storm. I did not lose how I did it. Ask, and I will show you.'
He has you run at the dark until the air cracks under your feet. On the third run it answers.
Yrsa scratches something unseen behind the ear. 'Things that will not stay put need a lesson in staying put. There is a bramble-word for it.'
She murmurs it once, then makes you say it to a patch of frozen bracken. It grows up around your boot, and she laughs.
Ask to be taught Flame Lance.
Rook shifts the duty board under his arm. 'Wardens carry a lance of fire for what the sword will not reach. I can show you the draw, if you can keep quiet while I do.'
He walks you through the draw slowly, hold and loose, and corrects your grip on the air twice. 'Good enough for a Warden.'
The Captain closes the ledger. 'The dawn falls where we say it falls. I do not teach it to just anyone, but you have not yet given me a reason to refuse.'
He marks a point on the courtyard with his boot and tells you to call the sun onto it. The flagstone is scorched by evening.
Ask to be taught Pyre Wall.
Cass does not move. 'The pedestal is not for you. The fire that guards it is a separate matter, and that I can teach.'
He draws a line in the dust and tells you to make it burn. It takes a while, and he watches every attempt.
Ask to be taught Ember Siphon.
The Hierarch lowers her lamp. 'There is a rite for those who have carried embers a while. It would slide off anyone who has not. You have, I think.'
The words take hold of you where the ash already has. The lamp gutters, and Selane smiles without warmth.
Ask to be taught Null Lance.
Ferris looks up, annoyed to be caught. 'The Archive has a lance in the margin of a book on unmaking. I have copied it out. You may as well have it.'
He turns the copied page toward you and reads it aloud in a flat voice. The words settle in your head like a coin in a purse.
Ask to be taught Arcane Shield.
Ask to be taught Gravity Well.
Coran blots a sheet. 'Two workings are kept in the annexe ledgers that were never meant for the shelves: a ward and a well. Which shall I copy for you?'
He copies the working onto a clean sheet, has you read it back, then burns the sheet. 'The Archive does not keep spare copies.'
Seren finally lifts her eyes. 'The old scholars had a step for crossing the sand between the shelves. Would you like it?'
She turns a page you were not supposed to be able to see. When you look up, you are on the far side of the reading desk.
Ask to be taught Lifebloom Totem.
Oda leans on the well-rope. 'A green thing planted at a well lives on other people's kindness. I know how to plant one that gives back.'
She has you press a seed into the sand and hum. It grows knee-high before she has finished scolding your tune.
Ask to be taught Knit Bone.
Ada tears a strip of linen without looking. 'Wounds and rot both. There is a way to knit a body and draw the rot out first. It is not pretty.'
She holds your wrist and shows you where to push. 'Rot first, then bone. Never the other way round.'
Ask to be taught Soul Tithe.
Ismene folds the proclamation. 'The Concord pays its debts in the coin it has most of. I can teach you the paying.'
It costs you something small and warm, and the working takes it. 'That is the tithe. Spend it well.'
Ask to be taught Grave Mark.
Corwen taps the dial. 'Everything here is marked with the hour it will stop. I can teach you to mark things that have not stopped yet.'
He shows you how to hold the mark in your mind like a number on a dial. Then he sets the clock a minute back for luck.
Black smoke stands over the north road and the Elder has stopped calling it a hearth fire. Ring the alarm bell, hold the square, and learn why a goblin warband is marching in daylight.

Goblins raid at night, in threes, and run when they bleed. This warband walked up the Kingsway at noon in step. The Elder wants the old bell by the Waystone rung and the square held until the town has barred its doors. Whoever is giving the orders has put a warband at the gate, and the town has you and a well.
The Elder stands by the Waystone in the Crown Square.
The Elder pointed north at the smoke and told you to ring the bell.
Ring the alarm bell by the Waystone
The bell hangs from a post beside the Waystone, a few paces from the Elder.
You rang the bell. Shutters banged shut across the square.
A carter lies against the trough at the north edge of the square. Optional.
You got the carter under a roof before the second wave.
Hold the square against the raiders
Stay near the well and the Waystone and cut down what reaches you. Holding your ground is what counts.
The raiders broke on the stones of the square and ran.
Tell the Elder it is over
Return to the Elder at the Waystone.
The Elder turned a black-iron token over in his fingers and did not like it.

Twelve years ago Kael Aldemar's sword-brother held the old Ashfall pass so the Emberguard could run. Black iron on a raider has sent you to look at it. Walk out to the Ashen Breach, see what was left there, and take it to Kael.

The Emberguard held a cut in the eastern hills until the Breach opened and the ash came down. Kael ran. Toren did not. The goblins took everything of his but the name, and somebody has kept his cairn ever since. The Citadel's scrip is stamped square. Something at that cairn is not.
Walk out to the Ashen Breach, the old Ashfall pass
East of the capital, in the hills past the mine road: look for the burnt cut and follow the dead grass.
The Breach is a wound in the hills. The old road runs through it and ends in sky.
Walk Kael out to the Breach
Optional. Kael is in your party: keep him with you on the walk and he will come to the cut. Do not leave him behind.
Kael walked the old road beside you and stopped at the mouth of the cut without being asked.
Find Toren's cairn in the cut
The cairn stands near the rubble heap at the western mouth of the cut.
Black stones, stacked shoulder high, and a name cut under a buckle: TOREN. HE HELD.
Take the black-iron token from the cairn
It lies on the cap-stone. Pick it up.
You took a round black token with a ring cut into it, broken at the top.
Show the token to Kael Aldemar
Kael is in the Crown Square, sharpening a blade that does not need it.
Kael would not keep the token. He thinks it was left for you.

Every cart that goes north passes the Wardens' post at the Crossway, and its captain has been told not to open the ones sealed for the Citadel. Walk the road north, hear Captain Fenn out, and open what he cannot.

Arms do not fall from the sky. Someone forged the spearheads the raiders carried, someone carted them north under seal, and someone at the Crossway counted them through. Captain Fenn has twelve wardens for a road that needs forty and a letter forbidding him to look in the wrong crate. There is a crate in the impound that nobody is allowed to open. You are not a warden.
Reach the Wardens' post at the Crossway
North up the Kingsway from the capital, past the north moor, to the gate with the towers.
The Crossway post: two towers, a gate, and a road that everything north has to use.
Put the banner's stamp to Captain Fenn
Fenn keeps the gate ledger by the door of the keep.
Fenn said he could not cut the seal on the impounded crate himself. He did not say you could not.
Open the sealed crate at the Impound Counter
The Impound Counter is at the east end of the post, beyond the Search Table, with the clerk standing over it.
Forty unfinished spearheads in garrison straw, each stamped twice: the Citadel's square, and a ring with a gap.
Find out who signed for the warband's arms
Take the stamps to Fenn. The Iron Syndicate broker at Hollowreach sells that kind of reading for gold, and the carter ledger at the Search Table is there for anyone quick.
The quartermaster's mark is the Marshal's. Now you know whose name is on the arms.

The Iron King's garrison sits on the spur above the capital, and the Marshal who signs for its arms has not been seen in a year. Climb to the Citadel, put out the signal fire before it calls the rest, and learn whether Orsolo Dray is a traitor or a prisoner.

The Citadel has two ways in: the front ramp, which is watched, and a postern in the west wall that a wounded scout may have mentioned. The brazier at the ramp keeps burning because it is a signal; every pair of sentries you cut down is replaced from the garrison hall until its smoke goes out. In the lowest cell of that hall sits the man whose name is on the arms, and what you do with him is yours to answer for.
Climb to the Iron Citadel's ramp
The Kingsway climbs to the spur from the capital's north gate. Keep to the road until you see the braziers.
The ramp is lined with black banners. Two braziers burn on it, and one of them is not for warmth.
Cut down the sentries at the ramp
They stand in pairs and relight the signal when hurt. Fight on the ramp, not in the open.
The ramp sentries are down. Their smoke still climbs.
Cut down the sentries at the postern
The scout's drain door lets you in behind the ramp. Only three stand between it and the court.
You came in by the drain door and the court was half empty.
The west ramp brazier is the one that never goes out. Put it out and the replacements stop.
The signal is out. Nothing is coming up the ramp behind you.
Find Marshal Orsolo Dray in the garrison hall
The cell is in the lowest level of the garrison hall, behind the court well.
Dray is chained in the lowest cell. He signed for the arms until the day he stopped.
Decide what becomes of the Marshal
Cut his chains or press him for what he knows. Speak to him again if you walked away.
You settled it. Whatever it was, you will be asked about it again.

The warband is broken, and every scrip, ledger and chained marshal points up the long road to the Ember Arena, where the first Flamebearer keeps his court of iron. Light the brazier, end it, and find out who has been watching from the gallery.

The Iron King was the first of the seven to be given the fire, and he has had a long time to decide what it is for. He holds the arena the way he held the Kingsway: closed to everyone but his own. The brazier at the sand's edge calls him out. Afterwards the Elder will want to hear all of it, including whatever you were not expecting.
Defeat the Iron King in the Ember Arena
Light the challenge brazier at the edge of the sand. In the second phase the garrison comes down to him: use the pillars.
The Iron King fell, and his ember lay on the sand like a second sun.
Speak to the rider in the arena gallery
A rider in black iron sits in the royal box above the sand. Walk up the gallery stair.
A tall rider in black iron watched the whole fight and spoke to you after.
Return to the Elder with what you learned
The Elder is at the Waystone in the Crown Square.
The Elder sang a counting rhyme about a stair, five who fell, and one who stayed to kneel.

Eleven survivors keep one fire beside the scar road, and the wolves that used to come to the fence in threes now come in thirties. Reach Last Hearth, hear Maeve Ashby out, hold the fence when the light drops, and see what Ada Voss can do with what the ash is doing to her patients.

Last Hearth is two roofless houses, a tent line and a fire. The beasts of the scar have always been dangerous, and lately they have become organised. Maeve will not leave and will not ask anyone to stay. Ada Voss burns what the ash gets into, and she is running out of things to burn.
Reach Last Hearth in the Ashen Wilds
Go through the Ashen Breach east of the capital, then follow the scar road to the one lit fire.
Last Hearth is a fire, two roofless houses, and eleven people who stopped expecting company.
Maeve sits by the fence, ten paces nearer the dark than anyone else.
Maeve said the wolves have started to come in thirties, standing in a ring, waiting.
Hold the fence at Last Hearth
Keep your back to the fire and fight at the fence line. They come in a ring, not a line.
The wolves broke at the fence and went back into the scar all at once, as if something had called them off.
Gather three healing herbs for Ada Voss
Healing herb grows in the green patches at the edge of the scar. Optional: Ada can make a calming smoke from it.
You brought Ada herbs for a calming smoke.
Ada works in the tent line by the second house.
Ada said the ash is calling both the wolves and her patients, and sent you to the Hunters' station.

Something on the plateau is calling the beasts of the scar, and Last Hearth is in the way. Climb to the Ash Hunters' station, read three tracks yourself, find where the herds meet, and decide what to do with them.

Hask Morrow counts packs the way other men count coin, and his numbers have stopped adding up: wolf and elk and boar walking the same road in step, at night, towards the plateau. Predator and prey do not do that. The three tracks he has staked are all he has. Where they meet is a herd the Hunters cannot name and a choice nobody else wants to make.
Climb to the Ash Hunters' station on Hunters' Rise
Follow the scar road north and east from Last Hearth, up the rise that watches the plateau road.
The Hunters' station looks down the whole scar road, and the road is full of ash.
Hask is at the rail of the rise with his hand over his eyes.
Hask has staked three tracks. He says the herds are walking in step.
Hask's first red stake is at the foot of the rise beside the scar road.
Elk and wolf, walking together. Neither ran.
The second stake is a little higher on the rise, where the road bends towards the wall.
The maw tracks keep station beside the elk. Every print points towards the wall.
The third stake is where the road meets the plateau ramp. Hask says the trail starts there.
A road trampled hand-deep, and a ring of stones set around a single antler.
Follow the tracks to where the herds gather
The three tracks join at the foot of the plateau ramp. Walk the trampled road to its end.
Forty animals of six kinds, standing shoulder to shoulder in the ash, waiting.
Decide what to do with the herd
Cull the herd, or break the call with calming smoke. The smoke needs three healing herbs.
You stood in front of them and picked.
Speak to the herd again if you walked away. Cull it, or burn three healing herbs for the smoke.
Cut down the herd's lead wolves
The wolves come first and the rest follow. Fight on the ramp road, not in the open ash.
The lead wolves are dead and the herd with them.
Keep the smoke burning while the herd settles
Stay upwind of the coals and keep the herbs burning. The wolves will test you once.
The smoke held. The herd forgot what it had been called to do.
The herds are quiet or gone, and the plateau road is open. The Beast Lord's brazier is cold and will take your flame. When he falls, tell Last Hearth the wolves will stop coming.

He was a Flamebearer who walked into the Wilds alone to cure the corruption at its root, and he did not walk out. Hask says the rot offered him strength that never tires and senses that never sleep, and he accepted a little at a time. The beasts go to him. Whatever is left of the man still answers to his name.
Ask Hask about the lights on the plateau road
Hask has been watching the plateau road since the herds went quiet. Optional.
Hask saw a rider in black iron stop at the foot of the ramp and ride back down.
Defeat the Beast Lord on his plateau
Light the blighted brazier at the head of the ramp. In the second phase he calls his pack, and in the third the scar answers.
The Beast Lord fell, and the Wilds went quiet the way a forest does when the hunter has gone.
Tell Maeve the plateau is quiet
Maeve is at the fence at Last Hearth.
Maeve said she may sleep a night through for the first time in thirty years.

The clans of Frostfang Reach have shut their hold to the south, and the three scout cairns on the north ridge have gone dark. The Storm Tyrant's motes ride the high passes. Reach the Clan Hold, draw flint and oil from Sigrun, relight the cairns, and be standing in the hold when the storm answers.

A dark cairn is a hole in the hold's eyes. It is how the vale sees weather coming and how the eight clans know to wake, and all three went out in the same moon. The Stormbound do not ask for help, and Hjalvar is not asking now; he is simply failing to turn you away. Sigrun counts oil in lamp-fulls and will not part with it for nothing, so she will want your name on her tally.
The Frostfang door is at the north end of the Ember Crown. Follow the Stormbound Vale road to the hold at its head.
The hold's gate was shut. It opened for you, narrowly.
Hjalvar sits by the moot ring in the middle of the hold.
Hjalvar said the north cairns have gone dark, all three in one moon.
Draw cairn oil and flint from Sigrun Ironhand
Sigrun keeps the stores by the long shed. She counts twice.
Sigrun counted the oil out twice and wrote your name beside it.
The first cairn stands on the rise where the north road leaves the hold.
The south cairn burns small and white.
Relight the middle scout cairn in the pass
North of the hold the road climbs into the pass. The second cairn is on the wind-scoured saddle.
A scout's mitten was frozen to the rim of the middle cairn. You left it where it was.
Relight the north scout cairn on the glacier
The last cairn is on the blue ice at the head of the pass.
All three cairns burn. Far to the north-east, something blue answers them.
Hold the Clan Hold when the storm answers
Fall back to the moot ring and fight with the shield wall at your back. The motes are fast and fragile: do not chase them.
The storm broke on the hold's shield wall. Hjalvar took a bolt through the shoulder and stayed on his feet.

The storm took Hjalvar's shoulder, and the clans will not march on the Stormcrown behind a chief who cannot climb. Two men claim the right to lead them: the hold's own chief, and the exile who lost a hand to his judgement. Both want the one thing the clans cannot give themselves: a stranger's hand on the moot stone.

The Stormbound's law is older than the hold: a chief who cannot lead into the storm names who will, or the clans do not go. Hjalvar would hold the passes and let the Tyrant's storm wear itself out on the wall. Halvar One-Hand would take a small party up the old winches at Stormfall and be at the Stormcrown before the next storm rises. Either way, someone has to put the ember on the stone.
Hjalvar is on the bench by the moot ring, shoulder bound.
Hjalvar would hold the passes and let the storm break itself on the wall.
Halvar's fire is outside the hold's gate, a little too far away to be an accident.
Halvar would take a small party up the old winches and be at the Stormcrown by morning.
Lay your hand on the moot stone
The moot stone stands in the middle of the moot ring. The eight clans are waiting.
You stood at the stone with eight clans watching.
Stand at the moot stone again if you walked away. Hjalvar holds; Halvar strikes.
The stone has been named. The clans moved.
Hold the Stormcrown road while the clans climb
Stand in the track-head under the spire. The clans climb behind you, slowly, and the storm will try the line.
The clans climbed behind your shield wall and the storm did not break it.
Crank the first winch at Stormfall
Two old winches stand at the head of the Stormfall track. Halvar says a Syndicate crew oils them every year.
The first winch turned as if it had been waiting for you.
Crank the second winch to the Stormcrown ledge
The second winch hauls the lift up the last stretch of cliff.
The lift shuddered up past old iron rings, and the spire was at arm's length.

The road to the Stormcrown is open and you stand under the spire. The Third Flamebearer comes down at the challenge brazier. When he falls, tell whoever holds the Stormbound hearth that the sky is quiet.

The Storm Tyrant came home from the Celestial stair to find his clan hold burned by men who swore they were saving it, and he has been answering them with lightning for four hundred years. The Stormbound call him the storm and do not say his name. The clans did not go to the Stormcrown when the weather began, and they will not go now, but they have stopped pretending he is only weather.
Break the Storm Tyrant at the Stormcrown
Light the Lightning Rod brazier on the duelling ground. His motes gather early: use the storm pillars for cover.
The Storm Tyrant fell, and for the first time in an age the Stormcrown was quiet.
A black-iron brazier stands cold a few paces from the Lightning Rod. The Ashen Knight will answer it. He yields before he dies: it is a duel, not a kill.
The rider in black iron yielded the field and said you would cross blades again.
Tell Hjalvar the storm is done
Hjalvar waits by the hearth in the Clan Hold.
Hjalvar asked you to eat at his hearth as kin.
Tell Halvar the storm is done
Halvar sits on the moot stone, which no exile has touched in twenty years.
The clans asked Halvar to take the high seat. He said he would think.

The oldest law in the Dominion is that the water at Saffra Wells is free. This season it tastes of ash. Reach the wells, hear Mother Oda, read the three gauge stones, follow the dead water to the Caravan Gap, and ask the people the Prophet's pilgrims have left behind.

Mother Oda Sarn has kept the wells for forty years and measured every season by three gauge stones the Archive set into the oasis wall. All three have gone grey. Her grandson walked south with the Prophet's people at midsummer, and the water has tasted worse every week since. Idrys Vane's caravans are turning back at the gap. Tamsin Reed walked the pilgrim track twice and will not do it a third time; she is the only one who will say why.
Go south through the Southmarch Gate and across the Caravan Gap. The oasis is the only green for a day's walk.
Saffra Wells: a ring of green, a ring of carts, and not one caravan loading.
Speak with Mother Oda at the wells
Mother Oda keeps the cistern at the centre of the oasis.
Mother Oda poured a cup of her own water into the sand. She has never done that.
Three gauge stones are set into the oasis wall: east, middle and west. Start with the east.
The east gauge is grey to the third line.
The middle stone is above the cistern's overflow.
The middle gauge is grey to the fourth line.
The west stone is nearest the road north.
The west gauge is black to the top. Whatever fouls the water comes from upstream, and from the south.
Follow the dead water north to the Caravan Gap
The one gap in the northern escarpment where the road from the Southmarch Gate comes in.
At the gap, two hundred pilgrims in red walk south in a line, each carrying a stoppered jar.
Vane is back at the wells with his turned-back carts.
Vane has hired four swords this week. He never needed one in twenty years.
Ask Tamsin Reed what the jars are for
Tamsin hides behind the cistern's far wall. She walked the pilgrim track twice.
The jars go south to be burned and come back as ash. The pilgrims tip it upstream and call it communion.

The ash in the wells comes from the Crimson Mission, where the Prophet's flock pours the altar's soot upstream and calls it communion. Walk the pilgrim track to the chapel and decide what becomes of the people who drink it.

The flock is not an army. It is two hundred people who were told that endings are a mercy, and some of them carry water to the altar twice a day because it is the only thing that quiets the voice. Deacon Haddan Voll keeps the chapel door. You can show them what the water does, you can speak to them in a voice they were waiting to hear, or, if you carry enough of the fire, you can tell them you already hear it too.
Walk the pilgrim track to the Crimson Mission chapel
South from the wells past the red flats, keeping to the pilgrim track. Do not enter the sanctum yet.
The chapel stands in front of the sanctum wall like a sleeve over a fist.
Speak with Deacon Haddan Voll at the chapel door
The deacon stands at the chapel door in red, with a ladle in one hand and a ledger of names in the other.
The deacon asked if you had come to tell him the wells taste of ash.
Decide what becomes of the flock
Speak to the deacon again if you walked away. Expose the water, turn the flock, or (if the fire in you is strong enough) tell him you already hear it.
Drive off the zealots who will not hear it
Half the chapel walked out. The other half stayed on its knees, and some of them are armed.
The zealots who stayed are down. The chapel door stands open on an empty nave.
Send Tamsin Reed to lead the leavers home
Tamsin waits at the wells with the pilgrims who left the chapel.
Tamsin took two dozen of them to the cistern and taught them to fetch real water.
Take the Prophet's seal from the sanctum door
The deacon left it on the sanctum door's latch, on a red cord.
The door breathed warm air in your face, and a voice that knew your name sounded relieved.
The flock has been dealt with and the altar fire will take your flame. The Fifth Flamebearer is waiting in the sanctum with his sermon. Break him, and tell Mother Oda how the wells will taste now.

He read in the great library for thirty years looking for a way to win that did not cost the world. Then a voice answered, patient and kind, and told him endings are a mercy. He does not think he betrayed anyone. He thinks he found the truth first. The wells were a sermon too: every cup a verse.
Break the Crimson Prophet in his sanctum
Kindle the altar fire in the sanctum. His zealots fight in the nave, and they mean it.
The Crimson Prophet fell, and his voice went on a while without him.
A black-iron brazier stands cold at the sanctum's edge. The Ashen Knight will answer it. He yields rather than dies.
The rider in black iron yielded a step at a time, smiling, and said he would not yield a third time.
Tell Mother Oda the voice is silent
Mother Oda is at the cistern in Saffra Wells.
Mother Oda poured the first cup from a clean draw.
Burn the warband's banner at the goblin camp
The camp is in the broken ruin on the western side of the Northern Wilds, a short walk from the Deadfall Lodge. The banner hangs from a pole of lashed deadfall.
The banner burned. Its corner carried the Citadel quartermaster's stamp.
Bryn is at the Iron Anvil in the Crown Square. He wants the ore in your hands, not in a ledger.
Bryn lit the forge from your ore: a forge that answers to the town, not the spur.
Tend the wounded scout on the King's Approach
A Dawnwarden scout lies in the ditch where the Kingsway climbs to the Citadel. She needs a health potion. Optional.
The scout told you about a drain door in the Citadel's west wall.
Mirela keeps the Green Retort in the Crown Square. Four sprigs, in your hand.
Mirela crushed one sprig, breathed it in, and told you to come back alive.
Follow the warband's road to the Ember Arena
The arena road leaves the mine road and runs north-east. The black-iron scrip stops at its gate.
The warband's road ends at the arena gate, and the gate is open.

The bell hangs from a post beside the Waystone, bronze gone green at the lip, its rope greasy with three generations of hands. You haul it. It cracks across the square and does not stop. Doors slam. Somewhere a mother is shouting a name. Far up the Kingsway the smoke turns towards the sound.
The rope is still swinging. Nobody is going to touch it again today.

A carter sits against the trough with both hands clamped on his thigh, his cart on its side behind him. 'Joss Harrow. They took the mule and left me the cart, which is the wrong way round.' He tries a laugh and it comes out as a cough. 'If somebody could get me off the stones before the next lot arrive, I would name a mule after them.'
Get an arm under him and carry him to the inn.
There is no time. Stay low.

He is heavier than he looks and complains the whole way, which you take as a good sign. The innkeeper's wife pulls him in by the collar and the door bars behind him. 'Mule,' he calls through the shutter. 'I meant it about the mule.'
The shutter opens a crack. 'Still no mule,' says Joss, 'but I am told you have a good chance of living long enough to be paid in one.'

Black stones, stacked shoulder high with no mortar and no gaps. Whoever built this had done it before, and more than once. A sword-belt buckle is set in the cap-stone, and cut beneath it with a dagger point, in letters gone soft with twelve winters of wind: TOREN. HE HELD. The grass around the cairn has been pulled by hand. Nobody comes out this far to tend a grave, and somebody does.
Take your hand off the stone.
The cairn is quiet. The wind has the pass to itself.

A disc of black iron the size of your palm lies on the cap-stone, set square as if with a rule. It is not Citadel scrip: those are stamped square and this is round, and where the Citadel's marks are crisp this one has been rubbed smooth by a thumb. Cut across its face is a ring, broken at the top like a door left ajar. It is cold in a way the wind cannot explain.

It is heavier than it should be. As your fingers close, the light on the ridge above the cut changes: a figure in black iron stands against the sky, utterly still, his helm turned towards the cairn, one hand on the pommel of a sword too long for any man to carry. He does not wave and he does not hide. You blink, and there is only ash light and bent grass. Whoever he is, he put this here, and he watched you pick it up.
The cap-stone is bare now, and paler where the token lay.

A pole of lashed deadfall with a banner of stitched goblin hide hanging from it, stiff with old blood. Goblins do not make banners. In the lower corner, sewn on with sinew, is a square patch of black-iron mail with a stamp pressed into it: the Citadel quartermaster's mark, the same one that was on the Elder's token.
Leave it. Count the camp first.
The hide curls and spits. The Citadel's stamp blackens last. Whoever this camp answers to will know by dusk that someone has been here, and what they looked at.
Ash on the ground and a charred pole. The camp's goblins keep well away from the spot.

The wax on the lid is the Citadel quartermaster's, square and red, and the clerk looks away while you work the chisel under it. Inside, in garrison straw, lie forty spearheads of unfinished black iron. The manifest tied to the lid says STORES, GARRISON. Each socket carries two stamps: the Citadel's square, and under it a ring with a gap at the top. The ring is not in any manifest.
Memorise the marks and close the lid.
The lid is back on the crate, and the wax is not going to look the same again.

The Search Table's carter ledger lies open under a paperweight made from a worn spur. Every consignment through the gate for a year, in the clerk's cramped hand, including the Citadel wax loads and the signature that cleared them. The clerk is arguing with a drover about a toll and has his back to you. The page you want is already half loose.
Tear out the page and pocket it.
Put the spur back. Not like this.

The sound is smaller than you feared. The page folds into your sleeve, and the quartermaster's signature on it is Orsolo Dray's. The drover wins his argument about the toll, which is the most anyone at the Crossway will notice today.
Walk away at a normal pace.
The ledger lies open to a page with a ragged edge. The clerk has not noticed yet.

A Dawnwarden scout lies in the ditch below the Kingsway with a bolt through her calf and a cloak pulled over her head like a tent. 'Not a patrol,' she whispers. 'Do not stand up. They are still watching the road from the spur.' She looks at what you carry. 'If you have a draught to spare, I have something to trade you for it. A door the Citadel forgot.'
I have nothing to spare. Stay hidden.

She drinks it like water and the colour comes back to her face by degrees. 'West wall of the Citadel, under the third buttress. There is a drain door for the garrison kitchens. The King forgot it because kings do not think about drains. Three sentries between it and the court, not six.' She tucks the cloak back over her head. 'Ilse Marrow. If you live, tell Fenn I kept my post.'
'Third buttress, west wall,' she whispers, and goes back to being a lump in a ditch.

A man in a marshal's coat with the rank cords torn off sits chained to a ring in the wall of the garrison hall's lowest cell. His boots are good, and he has not seen a razor in a month. 'You came up the ramp alone and the brazier is out. Either you are very good, or someone wants me to think so.' He rattles the chain. 'Orsolo Dray. I signed what they put in front of me for eleven years, and when they put the spearheads in front of me I stopped, and this is what stopping buys.'
What do you know about the ring with a gap?
Press him for what he knows.
Show your Dawnwarden badge and swear him to the Watch.
Offer his name to the Syndicate's ledger.
I am not done yet. Wait.

'The King. Not for love, for use. A king who keeps a warband on his own roads has an excuse to close the Kingsway to everyone else and take the tolls himself. The goblins get iron, he gets a siege he can ration. The captains drink at the arena's side gate: cut those and he has no road.' He laughs without breath. 'Nothing in this Citadel has been about the realm for ten years. It is about the King's weather.'
What do you know about the ring with a gap?

'I do not know the ring. I know the Citadel does not make it. I know the quartermaster's strongbox has a drawer I was never given the key to, and a clerk who never signs and never leaves. The King will not let anyone open the drawer.' His eyes slide away. 'That is all, and it is not much.'

The lock is old and the key hangs on a nail where the guards could not be bothered to hide it. The chain drops. Dray stands, and his knees almost betray him, and he does not let them. 'I will not say I am grateful. I will give you the roster, the postern drain and the arena's side gate, and I will tell the Black Wardens' captain that his marshal has been summoned to the Crossway to answer for the arms. Half of them will believe it. The other half will find they have somewhere else to be.' He walks out of the hall as if he owned it, which for a moment he does.

You do not cut the chain. You stand in the doorway, close enough that he has to look at what burns behind your eyes. You ask for the strongbox key. He says nothing. You ask for the roster, and say something else, quietly, and he gives you all of it in the order you asked, and a few things you did not. When he has done he does not look at you. 'The Wardens will come when the brazier does not answer. I will tell them I was no use to you.'
Take the strongbox key and the Citadel's purse.
The drawer opens on the third try. The purse is heavy, and what is under it is only paper. You leave him the chain.

You hold the badge where the lamp can find it, and the Marshal reads the sigil twice as if it might be a trick. 'The Watch does not take a man who signed for goblin spears.' 'The Watch takes a man who stopped signing,' you say, and turn the key on the nail. He does not weep. He stands very straight and says the Watch's oath into the dust of the cell floor, all of it, including the part about the weak. Then he walks out of the hall with his chain over one shoulder like a stole, and the sentries who never came do not come now.

You do not touch the chain. You say a number, and then a name, and Dray's face changes because the number is what the Ledger House pays for a marshal's confession and the name is yours. 'You are the Syndicate's now,' he says, with a sort of tired wonder. 'Good. At least they keep books.' He gives you the roster, the drain door and the strongbox key, in that order, and does not look up while he does it. The Ledger House will hear before the Watch does.
Take the key and the Citadel's purse.
The cell is empty. The chain lies in a pile where it fell, and the ring in the wall has a bright new scar where it was forced.
Dray does not look up. 'Whatever you wanted from me, you have it,' he says to the floor. 'Close the door on your way out.'

In the royal box above the sand, a rider in black iron has sat through the whole of it. He rises as you look, and the stone seat does not creak under him. He is very tall. His visor is down, and behind it the air is the colour of old fire.

'A rider. That will serve for now. I am told it is bad manners to give your name to someone who has not yet earned the answer.' He inclines his helm. 'I will give you one thing for nothing: do not trust the Elder's rhymes to the word. Every rhyme is somebody's apology.'

'You took it.' The voice is level and not unkind. 'Everyone does. It is the first fire and the oldest of those left, and it goes in like a coal into a dry hearth. You will find it keeps its own counsel.' A gauntlet taps the rail. 'He thought a wall around the world would keep it whole. He was not wrong about the wall, only about who it was for. We will speak again, Seventh. When you are carrying more.'

'You left it.' There is something in the voice that might be interest, or grief. 'Not many do, the first time. It lay there on the sand asking, and you walked past it like an unlit lamp.' A gauntlet taps the rail. 'The next ones ask louder. We will speak again, Seventh. I would like to see what you do when it is not the first.'
The royal box is empty. On the rail lies a round token of black iron with a ring cut into it, broken at the top, and it is warm.

The west ramp brazier is a basin of black iron on three legs, fed by a pipe from the garrison's own coal store, and it has not gone out in a year. You kick the feed pipe off its seat and bury the coals under a shield someone left on the ramp. The smoke thins to a thread and stops. Up on the walls a horn starts, and then stops too, the way a man stops who has remembered he is the only one still blowing it.
The basin is cold and black. Nothing climbs from it now.

Hoofprints of an ashfall elk, deep and even, cow and calf, walking. Over them, a pace behind and to the side, the prints of a dire wolf, also walking. The wolf's stride has not once broken to chase. A third set joins at the next stake: the broad splayed track of a thornback boar. They pace each other like a family on a road home.
Hask's red stake stands in the ash. The tracks go on without you.

The second track is old enough to have drifted. Elk and wolf again, and now a litter of maw tracks beside them: long toed, wrong, the prints of wolves that were something else once. They keep station with the elk. Every print points the same way, north-east, towards the wall. You find fur snagged in a thorn at one height that is neither wolf nor elk but both, as if one animal had worn two coats. Ash lies in every print like salt.
The second stake is leaning a little. The tracks beside it have not changed.

The third track is a road. Hundreds of prints, trampled to a cut a pace wide and hand-deep. At the edge where the tracks leave the scar, something has been laid in the dust: not a bone, not a pelt, but a ring of small stones set around a single antler, the way a person sets a table. The beasts did not do that. Or they did, and that is worse.
The ring of stones around the antler has not moved. The road leads on, north.

In a shallow of ash stands the herd: forty animals of six kinds, shoulder to shoulder, not grazing, not sleeping. At their heart a grey-eyed elk cow looks at you with perfectly ordinary elk eyes, and behind her a great dire wolf lies in the ash like a hound at a hearth. Antlers and fangs point nowhere. They are waiting for something to tell them to go on. The ember in your chest tugs at you, as though it knew the voice.
Cull the herd before it reaches him.
Cull the herd as the Hunters' book says, by the numbers.
Burn three healing herbs and break the call.

You do not pretend to speak to them. You draw, and the herd, which has been waiting for a voice, hears one: yours. They come at you in a wave with no fear in it, and it is the absence of fear that you will remember. When the ash settles there is a trampled shallow, a smell of copper, and an elk calf standing untouched among the dead, looking at you without understanding. Hask will want the count.
Gather what the Hunters will pay for.
Four good pelts, cut clean. You tell yourself that the Hunters keep records, and that records are a kind of mercy. The calf is still watching.

You drop the herbs on the coals and green-grey smoke rolls out sweet across the shallow. It is nothing the Beast Lord made and nothing he can unmake. The herd's heads come up one by one. The cow elk breathes it in, blinks, and for the first time in a month looks like an animal. The wolf sneezes. Ten breaths later the whole herd has simply stopped listening. A dire wolf lies down twenty paces from a calf and does not so much as look at it. Somewhere up the plateau, something notices that its voice has gone quiet.
Hask will not like it. The Hunters' manual has a page for culling and a page for tracking and no page at all for smoke. You will have to hold the coals while the herd settles.
The herd has made its answer in the ash. It does not need you to ask it again.

A cairn of flat grey stones with a stone lantern bowl on its crown, black and frozen. The oil in the bowl has set like candle fat. Storm char scars the windward face in a feathered pattern: something with a lot of lightning to spare has been here more than once. You break the ice with the flint haft, pour Sigrun's oil and strike. It catches on the fourth try, small, white and steady, and for the first time in a moon the hold has an eye on the south ridge.
The lantern burns small and steady. Somewhere below, a horn answers it.

The middle cairn sits on a wind-scoured saddle where nothing has grown in a thousand years. A scout's mitten is frozen to the rim of the lantern bowl, and the scout who wore it did not come home to pull it free. The bowl is split from rim to base. You wedge it with the flint haft, pour Sigrun's oil into the crack and strike, and the flame goes up crooked and holds. The wind tries it twice and gives up.
Leave the mitten where it is.
The crooked flame burns on. The mitten is still frozen to the rim.

Ice has grown over the north cairn in layers, so the lantern bowl sits inside a block of blue glass with a flame-sized hollow at its heart. You chip down to it with the flint haft and pour the last of Sigrun's oil into the hollow. When it catches, the ice lights from within and throws a pale bar of fire across the glacier. Far away to the north-east, high on the spire you cannot see, something answers with a blue that is not a lantern. The hold's horn begins blowing behind you, far down the pass.
The ice glows from within. The hold's horn has stopped blowing.

A waist-high stone worn smooth by eight clans' hands stands in the middle of the moot ring. Hjalvar has been helped to the bench beside it, grey in the face, his shoulder bound. At the ring's far edge, outside the firelight, Halvar One-Hand waits with his stump behind his back. The elders of the eight clans are watching. They have all seen the ember in you. None of them will say it aloud.
Lay your hand on the stone and name Hjalvar.
Lay your hand on the stone and name Halvar.

'Hjalvar, then.' Your voice is not loud. The stone is warm under your palm. The elders shift, and one by one they look at the chief instead of at you. Hjalvar does not smile. 'We go up as a wall. Slowly, with the shamans in the middle and the young on the flanks. Three days of climbing, and it will cost two of the old men their breath. It will not cost us the hold.' He looks across the ring at the exile. 'You will not be judged twice, Halvar. Go home to your fire.' The exile bows to nothing and goes.

'Halvar.' The stone is cold under your palm. The elders gasp as one and Hjalvar closes his eyes. 'So,' he says, quietly. 'The ember chooses the hand I took. I will not gainsay it. The clans will not climb with me, but they will not stand in your way.' Halvar is already at your elbow, smiling the smile of a man who has waited twenty years to be wrong in public. 'Winches at Stormfall. Two of them, and a Syndicate crew has oiled them every year, so do not thank me too loudly. Three hours up, and the Tyrant will still be eating breakfast.' He holds out a purse. 'Syndicate coin, for the road. Take it or do not.'
The purse is heavy and warm from his hand. He watches you weigh it, and says nothing, which is a kindness. You will remember that you took it.
The moot stone is cold. The ring is empty, and the clans have gone about the business of climbing.

An iron drum bigger than a man, its crank worn bright, the cable running up the cliff into cloud. Someone has greased it this year. You lean on the crank and it moves, grudgingly, then easily, and far above you a platform begins to descend through the mist with a long iron song.
Lock the drum and move to the next.
The drum is locked and the cable hums in the wind.

The second winch hauls the lift the last stretch of cliff to the Stormcrown ledge. You step onto the platform and work the crank until your arms shake. It shudders up past ice and old iron rings and a dead scout's marker, and somewhere above, thunder walks on the spire like a man pacing. When the platform bumps home, the duelling ground is thirty paces away and the brazier on its west side is the only light.
The lift rests at the top. The cable sings softly.

A tablet of pale stone set into the oasis wall, scored with seven lines in the Archive's neat hand. Mother Oda has chalked her own readings beside each line for forty years: a long column of ones and twos. This season the water stain has risen to the third line and it is grey, not brown. Rub it and your thumb comes away silver-black. It is ash.
The east gauge still reads grey to the third line.

The middle stone sits above the cistern's overflow, where the water is deepest. The stain here is grey to the fourth line. The chalk beside it is Mother Oda's, and for the last week the numbers have been written with a shaking hand. Someone has scratched under the gauge in a child's letters: THE WATER TALKS AT NIGHT. A man's hand has tried to scrub it out.
The middle gauge reads grey to the fourth line. The scratched words are still under it.

The west stone is nearest the road north and the first to take whatever comes down the channel. It has gone black to the top line. This is not seasonal silt: seven lines of the Archive's careful measure and the stain has gone past all of them. Whatever fouls the water comes from upstream, and the channel runs from the south, from the red flats and the pilgrim track.
The west gauge is black to the top line. Nothing here has changed.

Deacon Haddan Voll stands at the chapel door in red with a ladle in one hand and a ledger of names in the other. He is perhaps forty and looks sixty. Behind him two hundred people kneel in rows facing a wall of heat, and the whole nave smells of warm water and burnt sugar. 'You walked the pilgrim track,' he says, kindly. 'Most of us did it on our knees. You have the look of someone who has seen the wells. Have you come to tell me they taste of ash?'
Show him the three readings from the gauge stones.
Lay the readings out as a reader of the Veiled Archive.
Walk into the nave and speak to the flock.
Tell him you already hear it too.
Show the Emberbound sigil and tell him you already hear it too.

You do not shout. You set the three readings on his ledger one on top of another, grey on grey, and tell him what is in the water he blesses: not the Prophet's voice, only ash from his own altar, poured upstream twice a day by people he trusts. For a long moment the deacon looks at the readings the way a man looks at a doctor's face. Then he turns to the nave and reads them aloud in the same kind voice he uses for the names. The rows do not rise. They look at the ladle in his hand. Someone starts to cry. Within the hour half the chapel is walking north with its jars poured out on the red flats. The other half stays on its knees and does not look at you.
Step aside and let them pass.

You set the three readings on his ledger, and under them the Archive's own gauge-tablet seal, which he has seen on the oasis wall since boyhood. 'The Archive does not ask for belief,' you tell him. 'It asks for the same measure, read twice, by two people who do not like each other.' The deacon reads the numbers aloud in his kind voice. When he stops, no one in the nave is looking at the wall of heat. Half the chapel is walking north with its jars poured out by dusk, and a girl in the last row asks the nearest of you, shyly, what a gauge is. The other half stays on its knees and does not look at you.
Step aside and let them pass.

You show the sigil you were given at the Emberbound's table and say it quietly: 'I hear it too.' The deacon's face opens like a door. 'The Brothers of the Flame sent one of theirs to the Mission before,' he says. 'They did not stay. You will.' He kneels, and the nave kneels with him. He lifts the chapel key from around his neck and puts it in your palm. 'The sanctum is open to you. He is waiting. He would like to speak before whatever comes after.'

You walk past him into the nave and no one stops you. You stand where the heat is worst and say nothing for a long time. Then you say their names back to them, the ones he has in his ledger, not the ones the voice calls them. They look at the one who knows their names. 'The voice speaks to everyone,' you tell them. 'It asked me too. I said no. You can do the same.' Some weep. Some look at you the way they used to look at the wall of heat, and that frightens you more than the weeping. Tamsin Reed, who followed you down the pilgrim track, begins to hand out water from a cistern jar. Real water. The first cup is yours.
Drink, and step out of the heat.

'I hear it too,' you say, and the deacon's face opens like a door. 'Seventh of the Flame. He said you would come. He said you would not need telling.' He kneels, and the whole nave kneels with him, two hundred people moving like a field of wheat. He lifts the chapel key from around his neck and puts it in your palm. 'The sanctum is open to you. He is waiting. He would like to speak before whatever comes after.' Behind you, the heat in the wall rises to meet the heat in you.
The deacon is not at the chapel door. The ladle hangs from a nail, and the nave is quiet in the way of a room that has made up its mind.
